entries.title: Reading a risk register for the first time
entries.description: A risk register is a list of what could obstruct the objectives, with a score, an owner and a decision on each. The columns that matter, and the four signs a register has stopped being maintained.
sources: ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The scoring, and what it is for
Four signs a register has stopped working
What to do when handed one cold

blocks.html:
A risk register is the list of things that could stop the organisation
achieving what it set out to do, each with a size, a named owner, and a
decision about what happens next.
It is the most-read artefact in the discipline and the most frequently abandoned. Both facts have the same cause: a register is cheap to start and expensive to keep honest.

items.html: A cause, an event and a consequence in one sentence. “Supplier X fails, our checkout is unavailable, we lose transactions and breach the SLA.” Not a topic — “supply chain” is not a risk.
How large it would be with no controls in place. Argued over more than it deserves; useful mainly for showing how much the controls are earning.
What is currently in place, mapped to the control inventory rather than described freehand.
The size after those controls. This is the number the appetite is applied to.
One named person who can authorise the treatment. Not a team, not a function.
Accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid — with a date and a target score if it is anything but accept.
When somebody last looked, and when they will look next.

blocks.html: Registers commonly carry more columns than this. They rarely carry fewer and remain usable.

blocks.text: The scoring, and what it is for

blocks.html:
Likelihood times impact, on whatever scale the organisation has documented — usually 5 × 5, giving scores from 1 to 25. See 1.1 for the matrix itself.

Precision is not the goal. Two competent assessors will land in adjacent cells, and that is fine. What matters is that the bands are defined in writing, that a score can be traced to the criteria that produced it, and that the same criteria were applied last quarter. A register whose scale lives in one person’s head produces numbers that evaporate when they leave.

The level of risk remaining after existing controls are taken into account. The
number appetite is tested against.

blocks.text: Four signs a register has stopped working

blocks.html:
Nothing has moved in two quarters. Scores that never change mean nobody is reassessing them. Real registers churn.

Every owner is a team. “Owned by: Engineering” means owned by nobody. When the treatment slips, there is no one to ask.

The treatment column reads “monitor”. Monitoring is not a treatment; it is the absence of one, written to avoid the accept decision that someone would have to sign.

Closed risks disappear. A risk that was accepted and later closed should still be visible with its history. A register that only shows what is open cannot answer “did we know about this?”, which is the question asked after an incident.

blocks.text: What to do when handed one cold

blocks.html: Sort by residual score descending. Read the top ten statements and check each is a sentence with a consequence in it. Look at the review dates. Then find the appetite statement and check the top ten are actually above it — if they are not, either the appetite is set too high to be meaningful, or the register is only recording what was comfortable to write down.
Building a register from a blank sheet, and defending the scores in a committee, is the first module of GRC Mastery’s foundation track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Risk appetite vs risk tolerance
entries.description: Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around a specific objective. One is a stance, the other is a boundary.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

blocks.html: Appetite is the amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around a particular objective. Appetite is a stance; tolerance is a boundary on a number.

The two are used interchangeably in conversation and mean different things in every framework that defines them. The distinction matters at exactly one moment: when someone has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted.

Appetite is set once a year, by the board, and covers a category. We accept moderate operational risk to enter new markets quickly; we accept no risk that would compromise customer funds. It is directional and mostly qualitative.

Tolerance is the numeric edge on a specific objective. Availability must not fall below 99.5% in any calendar month. Cross it and something specific happens — an escalation, a treatment, a board paper.

Appetite tells you which risks you are in the business of taking. Tolerance tells you when a particular one has gone too far.

Most published appetite statements cannot be applied to a decision, which is the only test that matters. The three ways they fail:

Too abstract to test. “We have a low appetite for cyber risk” cannot resolve a specific question. Against what score, in what category, approved by whom?

No threshold. An appetite with no number attached cannot tell you whether the risk in front of you is inside it. The usable form names a residual score — no accepted risk above 12 without board sign-off — even when the category framing stays qualitative.

Uniform across categories. An organisation genuinely has different appetites for different things. A single statement covering all risk is either so permissive it permits everything or so restrictive it is ignored.

The maximum risk the organisation could absorb before it becomes unable to
operate. Appetite is set below capacity; the gap is deliberate.

The risk function scores an entry, produces a residual figure, and compares it against the appetite threshold for that category. Above it, the entry needs a treatment plan or a documented acceptance at the right level of authority. Below it, the entry is monitored on its review cycle.

Tolerance operates in a different loop, usually automated: a metric crosses a line, someone is notified, an issue is raised. It is the operational tripwire; appetite is the annual stance the tripwire was placed to protect.

Get the two the wrong way round — an appetite reviewed monthly, a tolerance argued about annually — and the function spends its time on the wrong meeting.

entries.title: Risk treatment options
entries.description: Four options and nothing else — accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid. What each commits you to, what evidence each needs, and which one "monitor" is really hiding.

sections.text: Why "monitor" is not on the list
What each treatment has to evidence
Sequencing when everything is above appetite

blocks.html:
There are four treatments and no others. Accept it, reduce it, move it to
somebody else, or stop doing the thing that creates it.

Every entry above appetite carries one of them, with an owner and a date. The value of the closed list is that it forces a decision: a risk with no treatment selected has not been decided about, however much has been written under it.

items.html: Take the risk as it stands. Requires an approval at the right level of authority, recorded with a date and a review point. Acceptance is a decision, not the absence of one.
Add or strengthen a control so the residual score falls. Requires a target score, a control that will exist, an owner and a date. Most treatments are this.

Move the financial consequence elsewhere — insurance, a contractual indemnity, an outsourced service. Note what does not transfer: the regulatory obligation and the reputational consequence almost never do.
Stop the activity. Rare, and usually the right answer exactly once, when the activity was never worth its risk.

blocks.text: Why "monitor" is not on the list

blocks.html:
It is the most common entry in a treatment column and it is the absence of a treatment, written to avoid the acceptance decision somebody would have to sign.

Everything is monitored — that is what the review cycle is. Writing “monitor” says the risk is being accepted without anybody putting their name to the acceptance, which is precisely the situation the register exists to prevent.

If the answer is genuinely accept, write accept, and get it approved. It is a respectable answer and auditors treat it as one.

blocks.text: What each treatment has to evidence

rows.a: Approval at the right authority, dated
Target score, named control, owner, date
The contract or policy, and what it excludes
rows.b: Cover still in force, limits still adequate

rows.a: Decision record, and confirmation the activity stopped

blocks.html: The right-hand column is the one programmes skip. A mitigation approved eighteen months ago, whose control was never built, still shows a reduced residual score in most registers — which makes the register actively misleading rather than merely stale.

The score a mitigation is expected to reach, stated when the treatment is
chosen. Without it there is no test for whether the treatment worked.

blocks.text: Sequencing when everything is above appetite

blocks.html:
A new programme frequently finds twenty entries above the threshold and capacity for four. The instinct is to lower the appetite until the list fits, which destroys the artefact.

The honest move is to treat four, accept the rest explicitly with a named approver and a shorter review cycle, and put the acceptance list in front of governance. That converts a resourcing problem into a decision the organisation has actually made, which is both defensible in audit and considerably more likely to release budget.

entries.title: Risk capacity, and the gap below it
entries.description: Capacity is the most risk the organisation could absorb before it stops functioning. Appetite is set below it deliberately, and the gap is the point.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The gap, and why it is deliberate

blocks.html:
Risk capacity is the maximum an organisation could absorb before it becomes
unable to operate. Appetite is set below it on purpose, and the distance between
them is the margin the business is choosing to keep.

Three terms sit on one line and are routinely collapsed into each other: capacity, appetite, tolerance. Capacity is a fact about the balance sheet and the licence. Appetite is a choice. Tolerance is a limit on a specific number.

Capacity is not a score. It is expressed in whatever would actually run out.

Money. The loss that would breach a covenant, exhaust the cash runway, or require an emergency raise.

Time. The outage after which contracted customers may terminate, which is usually written in your own service agreements and rarely read by the risk function.

Licence. The regulatory finding that would suspend an authorisation. Binary, and in regulated sectors it is the binding constraint regardless of the money.

An organisation that has never expressed capacity in at least one of these has no basis for saying its appetite is set conservatively — it has nothing to be conservative relative to.

blocks.text: The gap, and why it is deliberate

blocks.html:
Appetite below capacity leaves room for the risks you did not identify. That is its whole function. A programme that sets appetite at capacity is claiming its register is complete, which no register is.

How wide the gap should be is a board judgement, not a formula. What is reasonable to expect is that the board has been shown both numbers on the same page at least once, and has said the gap is the one it wants.

Applying a plausible severe scenario to the register and asking whether the
combined effect stays inside capacity. The only routine way to find out whether
the gap is real.

Rarely in daily work, which is why it goes missing. It matters at exactly three moments: setting appetite, approving a large acceptance, and after an incident, when somebody asks how close that came.

The third is when a function that has never articulated capacity discovers it cannot answer the only question the board wants answered.

entries.title: Business continuity, and how it differs from disaster recovery
entries.description: Business continuity keeps critical activities running, or restores them in an acceptable time, when disruption hits. Disaster recovery is its IT subset.
keywords: what is a business continuity plan
sources: ISO 22301:2019 — Security and resilience, business continuity management systems, requirements

sections.text: The line between continuity and disaster recovery
What a recovery time objective forces

blocks.html: Business continuity is keeping the organisation’s critical activities running, or restoring them within an acceptable time, when a disruption hits. Disaster recovery is the subset of that work concerned only with IT systems.

The two terms are used as synonyms and are not. Disaster recovery brings the technology back. Business continuity keeps the business function alive, by technology or by anything else that works — a manual process, an alternate site, staff held in reserve. One is a component of the other.

blocks.text: The line between continuity and disaster recovery

blocks.html:
Dimension Business continuity Disaster recovery
Scope The critical business activity The IT systems beneath it
The question it answers How does the function keep running? How do the systems come back?
Owns The business line that runs the activity IT or infrastructure
Trigger Any disruption to the activity Loss or failure of technology
Output Workarounds, alternate arrangements, roles Restored systems, recovered data

A disruption need not be technological to matter. A picket line, a burst pipe, a supplier failing, a key team unreachable — none of these is a disaster recovery event, and all of them stop the activity. Continuity has to cover the cases that have no server in them at all.
A plan is not a policy statement. It is the specific set of things that let a named activity survive, written so that someone under pressure can follow it.

items.html: The processes the organisation cannot be without for long, taken from the business impact analysis rather than guessed at.
The time within which each activity must be back, derived in the BIA at 3.7, not asserted by the plan.
What the activity actually needs to run — people, suppliers, systems and premises. A plan that lists only systems has missed most of them.
The workaround. How the activity runs while its normal means are gone, and who is trained to run it that way.
Who decides the plan is live, who does what once it is and who deputises when the first name is unreachable.
How staff, customers and regulators are told, with contact routes that do not depend on the failed system.

blocks.text: What a recovery time objective forces

blocks.html:
The target time within which a critical activity must be restored after a
disruption, set shorter than the point at which the harm becomes unacceptable.
Derived in the business impact analysis, not chosen by IT.

An RTO of four hours on order processing is not a statement about servers. It forces a set of arrangements to be standing by before the disruption: staff who can be reached and trained on the workaround, an alternate way to take orders that does not route through the failed system, and suppliers who have agreed to the same window. If any of those takes six hours to stand up, the four-hour RTO is fiction. The number is only as real as the slowest dependency behind it.

Never exercised. A plan that has not been walked through is an assertion, not a capability. The first invocation is not the moment to discover the alternate site has no network drops or the workaround needs a licence nobody bought.

RTOs asserted with no BIA behind them. A recovery time picked to look reassuring, rather than derived from what the activity actually needs, sets a target the arrangements were never built to hit.

A plan written for the building, not the process. Evacuation and premises cover is not continuity. If the plan says where people go but not how the work continues once they are there, the activity still stops.

Contact lists that rot. People move, numbers change, deputies leave. A list maintained once at authoring is wrong within a year, and it is wrong at exactly the moment it is needed.

items.q: Is business continuity the same as disaster recovery?
items.html: No. Disaster recovery restores technology — systems, data, connectivity. Business continuity keeps the critical activity running by whatever means, which may be a manual workaround, an alternate site or standby staff that never touch the failed system. Disaster recovery is one input to continuity, not a synonym for it.

items.q: How often should a continuity plan be tested?
items.html: On planned intervals and again after any material change to the process, its people or its dependencies — ISO 22301 frames the cadence that way rather than as a fixed figure, though annual is the common floor in practice. The test need not be a full invocation each time; a tabletop walkthrough of one plausible scenario exposes most of the gaps that matter, at a fraction of the cost.

items.q: Who owns business continuity?
items.html: The business line that runs the activity owns its continuity, because only it can authorise the workaround and carry it out. A central function may coordinate the programme, set the method and hold the plans, but it cannot own the recovery of a process it does not run.

entries.title: Business impact analysis, and the numbers it sets
entries.description: A business impact analysis ranks activities by how fast each must return, producing the RTO, RPO and MTPD a continuity plan is sized against.
sources: ISO 22301:2019 — Security and resilience, business continuity management systems, requirements
ISO/TS 22317:2021 — Security and resilience, business continuity management systems, guidelines for business impact analysis

blocks.html: A business impact analysis works out which activities matter most and how quickly each must be back, producing the recovery time objective (RTO), recovery point objective (RPO) and maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD) the whole continuity plan is sized against.

It is the numbers engine under business continuity. Everything downstream — recovery strategy, standby capacity, the plan’s own deadlines — is scaled from what the analysis produces. Get the numbers wrong and the plan is either unaffordable or too slow, and there is no way to tell which until it is used.

items.html: The target time to restore an activity after disruption. Miss it and the activity has been down longer than the plan promised anyone it would be.

The maximum data loss that is tolerable, expressed as a length of time — the point back to which data must be recoverable. An RPO of fifteen minutes means never losing more than the last fifteen minutes of work.
The elapsed time after which the impact of not resuming becomes unacceptable. The hard outer boundary the RTO has to sit inside.

blocks.html: The ordering is a constraint, not a preference. RTO must be set shorter than MTPD. Set them equal, or the wrong way round, and the plan is scheduled to finish restoring the activity at exactly the moment the damage has already become unacceptable — it misses its own deadline by design.

The maximum tolerable data loss, stated as a length of time rather than a volume.
It sets how often data must be backed up or replicated: a fifteen-minute RPO
forces backups no more than fifteen minutes apart.

Four steps, in order.

List the activities. Every activity the organisation performs, not the systems behind them. Payroll is an activity; the payroll server is a dependency of it.

Grade impact against time. The same outage is trivial at one hour and fatal at one week. Impact is assessed as a curve that grows with the length of the disruption — financial, legal, reputational and safety impact each plotted across hours, days and weeks. This is the step most often skipped, and skipping it is what makes the resulting numbers meaningless.

Map dependencies. For each activity, the people, systems, suppliers and premises it needs to run. An activity cannot recover faster than the slowest thing it depends on, so an RTO shorter than its dependencies’ is a fiction.

Set the numbers from the curve. The point where impact turns unacceptable fixes the MTPD, and the RTO is set shorter than it, with margin to spare. The RPO answers a separate question — how much data the activity can afford to lose — and is read from the tolerable gap between backups, not off the downtime curve. The numbers come from the impact, not the other way round. A programme that picks a comfortable RTO first and writes the impact analysis to justify it afterwards has the whole process reversed.

Take one activity — customer payment processing — with an RTO of 4 hours, an RPO of 15 minutes and an MTPD of 24 hours. Each figure forces something concrete.

Figure What it forces
RTO 4 hours Payments must be recoverable within four hours of an outage, so the standby capacity, failover and trained staff to do it have to exist and be tested.
RPO 15 minutes Transaction data must be captured or replicated at least every fifteen minutes, so no more than a quarter-hour of payments is ever lost.
MTPD 24 hours Past a full day down, customers give up and move on, and the lost revenue stops being recoverable at all.

The RTO buys margin against the MTPD. Four hours against a twenty-four-hour tolerance leaves room for a recovery that runs late without crossing the point of no return. That margin is the reason RTO is set below MTPD rather than at it.

Everything is rated critical. When every activity is top priority, every RTO collapses to one hour and the plan demands more simultaneous recovery than any organisation can fund. A BIA that does not force a ranking has not been done.

Impact is never graded against time. A single severity score with no time axis cannot locate the MTPD — the moment impact crosses from tolerable to not — and without that point there is nothing for the RTO to be set inside. Without the curve the numbers are guesses wearing a decimal point.

It is run once and shelved. A BIA completed for certification and never revisited describes an organisation that has since moved on — activities, suppliers and volumes have all changed. It is reviewed at planned intervals and after any material change to the business — commonly at least once a year in practice.

items.q: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
items.html: RTO looks forward: how quickly the activity must be running again. RPO looks backward: how much data, measured in time, can be lost when it returns. RTO is about downtime, RPO is about data loss, and the two are set independently — a payment system can tolerate hours of downtime but almost no lost transactions.

items.q: Who provides the data for a BIA?
items.html: The people who run the activity, not the risk or continuity function. The business owners state what breaks and when it starts to hurt; continuity facilitates, challenges the answers and records them. Numbers set by the continuity team alone are the ones the business disowns during an actual incident.

items.q: How often should a BIA be redone?
items.html: At least annually, and on any material change — a new product, an acquisition, a moved supplier or a changed regulatory obligation. A BIA is a snapshot of a moving business; left unrevised it goes quietly out of date and takes the whole continuity plan with it.

entries.title: Third-party risk management (TPRM)
entries.description: Third-party risk management identifies, tiers and monitors the risk suppliers and vendors carry into the organisation you no longer directly control.
sources: ISO/IEC 27036-2:2022 — Cybersecurity, supplier relationships, Part 2: Requirements
NIST SP 800-161r1 — Cybersecurity supply chain risk management practices for systems and organizations

sections.text: Tiering: not every supplier gets the same scrutiny

blocks.html: Third-party risk management is identifying, tiering and monitoring the risk that suppliers and vendors carry into the organisation — because a control you depend on is now operated by someone you do not manage.

Treat “vendor”, “supplier” and “third party” as one population here. The words sort procurement paperwork; the risk they carry is the same, and so is the technique for handling it. Every supplier operates a service or control the organisation has chosen to run outside its own walls, and the register at 3.1 carries the consequences when one fails.

blocks.text: Tiering: not every supplier gets the same scrutiny

blocks.html:
The first move is to sort the population by what each supplier could actually hurt — access to production data, position inside a continuity RTO, regulatory exposure — and never by what it costs. Depth of due diligence then scales with the tier, so effort lands where the exposure is.

Tier What the supplier can hurt Due-diligence depth
Critical Holds production or customer data, or sits inside a recovery time objective Full assessment: security review, financial stability, evidence-backed or on-site audit, named executive sponsor
Important Regulatory exposure, or access to limited personal data Questionnaire with evidence sampled, contractual controls verified before signing
Routine No sensitive data, readily replaced Standard terms, a register entry and light reassessment by exception

A cheap supplier with a live connection to production belongs in the top tier. A large invoice for stationery does not. Spend is the wrong axis.
TPRM is not an onboarding gate. It runs from before the contract to after it, and each stage leaves evidence the next one depends on.

items.html: The assessment done before signing, scaled to tier — security posture, financial stability and regulatory standing, judged on the evidence behind the answers rather than the answers alone.
The rights that must survive the honeymoon: a right to audit, a breach-notification window measured in hours and limits on which sub-processors may be used and what data they may touch.
Reassessment on a cadence set by tier, plus watching for the events that change the tier — a breach, a change of control, a service moved offshore.
Access revoked, credentials killed and data returned or destroyed with evidence. The step skipped most often, and the first one an auditor checks.

blocks.html: The risk that arrives through your supplier’s own suppliers — the parties you have no contract with and cannot assess directly. It is managed indirectly, by requiring each critical third party to control and disclose its own critical dependencies.

Due diligence done once. The assessment is completed at onboarding, filed and never repeated. The supplier’s risk is frozen at the one moment it was lowest — before it had access to anything.

Tiering by contract value. The largest invoice gets the deepest review while a cheap supplier with production access is waved through. That is usually where the incident comes from.

A questionnaire nobody reads. Two hundred answered questions, no evidence sampled, no follow-up on the “no” that should have stopped the deal. A completed questionnaire is not assurance; a verified one is.

Concentration risk. Ten services behind one provider, each passed on its own and nobody added them up. Aggregate exposure is the risk function’s job — see 3.0 — not the procurement queue’s.

items.q: What is the difference between vendor risk and third-party risk?
items.html: Little worth managing to separately. “Vendor” usually names a supplier paid for a product or service; “third party” is the wider set that also includes partners, agents, resellers and anyone else operating a control on your behalf. The techniques — tiering, due diligence, monitoring, offboarding — are identical, so both are handled as one population. The distinction that does matter is risk versus compliance, covered at 1.9.

items.q: What is fourth-party risk?
items.html: The risk from your suppliers’ own suppliers. A cloud host depends on a data-centre operator; a payroll processor depends on a hosting provider you have never named. You hold no contract with them and cannot assess them directly, so the control is contractual: require each critical third party to manage, and disclose, its own critical dependencies.

items.q: How often should a third party be reassessed?
items.html: On a cadence set by tier, not a single calendar rule. Critical suppliers annually at least, and immediately on a trigger — a breach, a change of control, a service relocated. Routine suppliers can run on a longer cycle or by exception. A flat “every three years for everyone” repeats the tiering-by-spend mistake: it decouples effort from risk.

blocks.html: Standing up a supplier-tiering model and a due-diligence workflow from a blank sheet is one track in GRC Mastery’s vendor-risk course. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Emerging risk, and keeping a horizon scan honest
entries.description: An emerging risk is one whose likelihood or impact cannot yet be scored reliably. Horizon scanning tracks it on a watch-list until it can.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

blocks.html: An emerging risk is one whose likelihood or impact is not yet understood well enough to score reliably — new, fast-changing or not yet materialised. That is exactly why it resists the ordinary register, which assumes every risk can already be sized.

The label is useful and abused in roughly equal measure. Held to its meaning, it names the small set of risks that a scoring scale genuinely cannot yet handle. Used loosely, it becomes a place to put anything nobody wants to treat.

A likelihood-times-impact score needs a basis to stand on: history, comparable events or documented criteria to reason from. An emerging risk has none of these yet — that absence is what makes it emerging. Force a number onto it and the number manufactures a precision that does not exist.

The failure is not that the register rejects the risk. It is that the register absorbs it. An unfamiliar risk with no track record almost always scores low, and a low score on an ordinary register (see 3.1) is where a risk goes to be forgotten. Nothing looks wrong. The item is on the list, near the bottom, never reviewed.

Horizon scanning earns its place only when it feeds a decision. Three things separate a real scan from a slideshow.

Named sources. Regulatory pipelines — consultations and draft legislation before they bind. Incidents in the sector, especially at comparable organisations. Technology shifts that change what an attacker or a competitor can do. Each source has one person responsible for reading it.

A fixed cadence. A scan that happens when someone remembers is not a scan. Quarterly is common; the interval matters less than that it is booked and minuted.

A watch-list, held apart. Emerging risks sit on a list of their own, kept separate from the register so they are not forced into a score, but put in front of the same committee that reads the register. An item is promoted into the register the moment it becomes scorable — the first comparable incident, the first draft rule with a date attached.

The routine of looking past the current register at signals that may become
risks: regulatory pipelines, sector incidents and technology shifts. Its output
is a dated watch-list, not a score.

Two things go wrong, and they pull in opposite directions.

The label as a hiding place. A risk that is perfectly scorable gets called emerging so that no owner, no treatment and no date have to attach to it. Emerging quietly becomes a synonym for untreated. The test is blunt but not absolute: if a close comparable has already played out somewhere, the risk can usually be sized from it, and calling it emerging is often just a way to avoid doing so. The honest exception is a familiar risk whose scale, context or trajectory has shifted enough that the old comparables no longer size it.

The scan nobody acts on. The opposite failure. A tidy watch-list is produced each quarter, noted and filed. Nothing is ever promoted, and nothing is ever struck off as no longer credible. A scan with no route into the register and no route off the list is theatre with minutes.

items.q: What is the difference between an emerging risk and an existing one?
items.html: An existing risk can be sized. There is history, criteria or a comparable event to reason from, so it carries a likelihood, an impact and a place on the register. An emerging risk cannot be sized yet — it is new, moving too fast to pin down, or has not materialised anywhere. The dividing line is not how novel it feels but whether a reliable score is possible.

items.q: How do you score an emerging risk?
items.html: Ideally, not yet — that is the whole point. Scoring it prematurely invents a number with no basis and usually parks it low. Instead, hold it on a watch-list with what is known, what would change the picture and what is being watched for. Promote it into the register, and score it, the moment there is a basis: a comparable incident, a draft rule with a date, a first loss.

items.q: Who owns horizon scanning?
items.html: The risk function owns the process — the sources, the cadence and the watch-list. It does not own the subject-matter judgement behind each entry. Reading the regulatory pipeline sits with compliance or legal; reading sector incidents sits with security or operations. See 3.0 for the split between owning a process and owning the content that runs through it.

entries.title: Policy waivers and exceptions
entries.description: A policy waiver is a documented, time-bound decision to run out of compliance with a control, backed by a compensating control and a named approver.
sources: ISO 31000:2018 — Risk management, guidelines (retaining a risk by informed decision)

Exception- and waiver-register conventions — expiry, compensating control, approver at the right level — are control-governance good practice drawn from security and audit practice, not a single mandated standard

blocks.html: A policy waiver, or exception, is a documented, time-bound decision to run out of compliance with a control or policy: an accepted risk with a compensating control and an expiry date, not a quiet permanent gap. It is the risk acceptance of 3.3, made explicit.

A waiver does not weaken the policy. It records, in one place and above someone’s signature, that a specific gap is known, is bounded and will be looked at again. The alternative is not compliance — it is the same gap, undocumented and owned by nobody.

An alternative control that reduces the exposure the waived control would have
covered, for the life of the waiver. It does not restore full compliance; it
holds the risk down until the gap is closed or re-decided.
A waiver missing any of these is not an exception. It is a gap with a note attached.

items.html: Which control or policy clause is not being met, stated precisely. “The password policy” is not a gap; “MFA on the legacy billing console” is.
Why the exception is needed — a system that cannot meet the control, a delivery deadline, a disproportionate cost — recorded so the next reader can weigh it without asking.
What holds the exposure down while the gap is open. Named, not promised.
One person at a level that matches the size of the risk. A larger exposure is signed higher, by someone who could accept the underlying risk itself.
The date the waiver ends and the gap returns for a fresh decision.
When the exception is checked before that date, in case the reason has gone away sooner.

blocks.html:
A waiver with no end date is not an exception. It is a silent, permanent change to the policy that nobody approved as permanent. The control still says one thing; the organisation quietly does another; and the record that this was ever a decision fades with the person who made it.

The expiry forces the gap back onto a desk for a fresh decision, rather than letting the exception become the new standard by default. When the date arrives the choices are three: close the gap; renew the waiver, with the reason and the compensating control re-examined; or accept the risk permanently through a documented change to the policy itself. Doing nothing is not one of them. That is the whole purpose of the date.

Every waiver lives in one register, not in the email that approved it: an exception register holding every open exception with its expiry, its approver and its compensating control, in one place that can be counted. It is a sibling of the issue log the risk function keeps (see 3.0), not the same book.

Counted and trended, the register says something the individual waivers do not. A rising number of exceptions against one control is a signal about the control, not about the teams asking to bypass it: either it is written more tightly than the organisation can meet, or the policy behind it is wrong. A waiver count that only ever grows is a policy being repealed one exception at a time, without anyone deciding to repeal it.

items.q: What is the difference between a waiver and risk acceptance?
items.html: A waiver is a form of risk acceptance — the acceptance decision from 3.3 — applied to a named control or policy and bounded by an expiry date. Plain acceptance can stand open-ended; a waiver is the same decision made time-bound and tied to a specific gap, so it returns for review rather than lasting forever by omission.

items.q: Who should approve a policy waiver?
items.html: One named person at a level that matches the exposure being accepted. A small, well-compensated gap can be signed by the control owner; a material one belongs to the risk owner or an executive — the same person who could accept the underlying risk. The approver must sit high enough to own the consequence if the compensating control fails.

items.q: What happens when a waiver expires but the gap remains?
items.html: The exception is out of force the moment it expires, so the organisation is now non-compliant with no decision behind it. Three routes close that: fix the gap; renew the waiver, with the reason and compensating control re-examined; or accept the risk permanently by changing the policy through 2.1. An expired waiver left open is the exact failure the expiry date exists to prevent.

entries.title: Key risk indicators (KRIs), and how they differ from KPIs
entries.description: A key risk indicator is a leading metric that warns exposure is moving toward appetite before it becomes an incident, unlike a lagging KPI.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: How a KRI differs from a KPI
What makes a KRI worth having
A worked example, tied to appetite

blocks.html: A key risk indicator is a metric that warns that risk exposure is moving toward, or past, appetite — where a key performance indicator measures progress toward an objective. A KRI is chosen to lead, so the warning arrives while there is still time to act.

The distinction is not simply leading versus lagging. What separates them is subject: a KPI tracks performance against an objective, a KRI tracks the exposure behind a risk. A KRI is then chosen so that it moves early — watching the drivers of a risk while there is still time to act, rather than its residual score on the register 3.1 after the fact.

blocks.text: How a KRI differs from a KPI

blocks.html:
The two are routinely confused because both are numbers on the same dashboard. They answer different questions: one tracks the exposure behind a risk, the other progress toward an objective.

Key risk indicator Key performance indicator
What it measures Exposure moving toward a limit Progress toward an objective
Direction in time Chosen to lead — warns before the event Usually lagging — records after
What it is tied to An appetite threshold A performance target
The question it answers Is a risk building? Was the objective met?
Example Privileged accounts without MFA Uptime achieved this quarter

The same raw figure can serve as either, depending on what it is tied to. Uptime against a target is a KPI; the number of near-misses trending up beneath that uptime is a KRI.

blocks.text: What makes a KRI worth having

blocks.html: Most indicators on a risk dashboard are neither leading nor actionable. Four properties separate one that earns its place from one that fills a cell.

items.html: It moves before the event it warns about, not after. A count of incidents already suffered is a scorecard, not an early warning.
A written level at which green becomes amber and amber becomes red. Without it the number has no meaning and can never be breached.

items.term: Owned by someone who can act
items.html: A named person, not a function, who is accountable for the response when it breaches. An indicator no one owns is watched by no one.
A breach triggers a specific, pre-agreed response, not a discussion about whether to have one.

blocks.text: A worked example, tied to appetite

blocks.html: The level at which an indicator stops being informational and demands a response. It is set relative to appetite 3.2, so a breach means exposure has moved to where the organisation already said it would act.

Take a single control risk: privileged accounts left without multi-factor authentication. The indicator is the proportion of privileged accounts with no second factor, and appetite is expressed as bands — illustratively, green below two per cent, amber at five per cent, red at ten per cent. The figures are examples; the real ones come from what the organisation has decided it can carry.

Amber is where the indicator earns its place. Crossing it is not an incident, so nothing has failed yet, but it triggers a named response: the account owner is notified, the coverage gap is closed within a fixed window and if the figure reaches red the exception is escalated to the risk committee. An indicator with none of that wiring behind it is a colour on a slide.

Chosen because they are easy to collect. The indicator that is trivial to pull from a system is rarely the one that predicts anything. Ease of collection and predictive value are unrelated, and optimising for the first buys a dashboard that measures nothing that matters.

No threshold, so nothing ever triggers. A number with no defined green, amber and red cannot breach. It is reported, noted and forgotten, quarter after quarter, because there is no line for it to cross.

A dashboard of green that never moves. Indicators that sit at green for a year are either measuring a risk that is genuinely dormant or, far more often, measuring the wrong thing. A board reporting pack 2.3 of unchanging green is a signal to re-examine the indicators, not reassurance.

items.q: What is the difference between a KRI and a KPI?
items.html: The difference is subject, not just timing. A KPI measures performance against an objective; a KRI measures whether the exposure behind a risk is building. A KRI is then deliberately chosen to lead, so it moves while there is still time to act, where a KPI usually confirms an outcome already fixed. The same figure can be either, depending on whether it is tied to a risk appetite threshold or a performance target.

items.q: How many KRIs should you have?
items.html: Few enough that each one is watched and acted on. A handful of indicators tied to the risks the board actually cares about beats dozens that no one owns. If a KRI has no defined threshold and no named owner, removing it loses nothing.

items.q: How do you set a KRI threshold?
items.html: Work back from appetite. The red line sits where exposure would breach what the organisation has said it will tolerate; amber sits far enough below it to leave time to act before red. Both are judgements, so record who set them and revisit them when appetite changes.

blocks.html: Designing indicators that actually predict, and wiring their thresholds to appetite, is worked through in GRC Mastery’s risk-reporting module. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Risk quantification, and when a number beats a heat map
entries.description: Risk quantification states exposure as a probable monetary loss and its spread, not a heat-map colour. It answers how much, which a red cell cannot.
sources: The Open Group, Risk Analysis (O-RA) Standard — the Open FAIR body of knowledge

sections.text: Qualitative and quantitative are not a hierarchy
What a quantified risk looks like

blocks.html: Risk quantification expresses exposure as a monetary range — a probable loss and its spread — instead of a colour on a heat map. It answers the one question a red, amber or green cell cannot: how much.

blocks.text: Qualitative and quantitative are not a hierarchy

blocks.html:
Neither method outranks the other; each answers a different question. Qualitative scoring — the likelihood-times-impact heat map at 3.1 — triages breadth cheaply, ranking a whole register in an afternoon. Quantification costs more, and earns its place on the few decisions where a number actually changes the call: a large risk acceptance, a control-spend trade-off or a board question about whether exposure sits inside capacity (3.4).

The mistake is to treat one as the grown-up version of the other. A register quantified end to end is not more mature than a well-kept heat map. It is usually just more expensive.

blocks.text: What a quantified risk looks like

blocks.html:
A quantified risk is a loss, and a loss has two parts: how often the event happens and how much it costs when it does. Loss equals frequency times magnitude. Expressed honestly, each side is a range, so the output is a distribution — a most-likely figure with a spread around it — not a single number dressed up as certainty.

Money is the usual unit because it lets unlike risks be compared and weighed against the cost of treating them. A count of records exposed or hours lost is quantitative too; the financial form is simply the one that travels to a board.

The simplest form drops the spread and multiplies two point estimates. Annualised loss expectancy (ALE) is single loss expectancy times the annual rate of occurrence: a £2m loss expected once every ten years is an ALE of £200,000. It is a starting point, not the destination.

FAIR — Factor Analysis of Information Risk, standardised by The Open Group as Open FAIR — is the common open method for decomposing frequency and magnitude into parts that can each be estimated. It gives a shared vocabulary and a defensible structure. It does not manufacture data: the output is only ever as sound as the estimates fed into it.

The expected cost of a risk over one year: single loss expectancy multiplied by
the annual rate of occurrence. A single figure, useful as a first cut rather than
the whole answer.

False precision. A probability invented in a meeting does not become data because it carries a decimal point. A confident number built on guesses is more dangerous than an honest colour, because it travels further before anyone thinks to question it.

Quantifying everything. The effort is justified by the decision it informs. Running a full analysis on every line of the register spends the budget that the three decisions actually needing it should have had.

A model no one can explain. If the board that has to trust the number cannot follow how it was reached, the number carries no authority. Complexity that cannot be explained to the person signing is a cost, not a feature.

items.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative risk analysis?
items.html:
Qualitative analysis ranks risks on a descriptive scale — usually likelihood times impact rendered as a heat map — and is quick enough to run across an entire register. Quantitative analysis expresses a risk as a monetary loss, or a range of losses, and takes real effort to do well.

One sorts the population; the other sizes an individual decision. Most programmes need both, applied where each fits.

items.q: What is the FAIR model?
items.html: FAIR, Factor Analysis of Information Risk, is an open framework for quantifying risk in financial terms. It breaks loss down into loss frequency and loss magnitude, then decomposes each further so the parts can be estimated and recombined. The Open Group maintains it as Open FAIR. It is a way to structure the analysis, not a source of the underlying numbers.

items.q: Do you need to quantify risk?
items.html: Not for every risk. Quantify where a number changes a decision — a large acceptance, a spend trade-off, a capacity question (3.4) — and leave the rest on the qualitative heat map. Quantifying everything wastes the effort that the decisions genuinely needing it deserve.

entries.title: Running a risk workshop
entries.description: A risk workshop is a facilitated session that surfaces and sizes risks with the people who own the work. Its real output is the argument, not just the list.
keywords: how to run a risk workshop
sources: IEC 31010:2019 — Risk management, risk assessment techniques
ISO 31000:2018 — Risk management, guidelines (communication and consultation)

sections.text: The facilitation problems that ruin it
Turning a workshop into register entries

blocks.html: A risk workshop is a facilitated session that surfaces and sizes risks with the people who own the work. Its real output is the argument in the room, not just the list that leaves it. Brainstorming is one of the techniques IEC 31010 catalogues, and a workshop applies it in a structured form.

A workshop earns its place when the risk cannot be read off a document — when it lives in the heads of the people doing the work and has to be talked out. The value is proportional to how honestly the room disagrees.

The room needs two things at once: first-line owners, who know where the work actually breaks, and second-line facilitation, who keep the conversation honest and stop it drifting. Balance is the whole problem. Too senior and nobody will contradict the person who signs the appraisals; too junior and nothing decided in the room can be committed to afterwards.

The workable mix is people close enough to the process to see the failure and senior enough to own the treatment, run by a facilitator who owns none of it. Keep it small — six to ten — so every voice has room. A group larger than that turns into an audience.

blocks.text: The facilitation problems that ruin it

blocks.html: Most of what wrecks a workshop is social, not analytical. Four failures recur.

items.html: The first number spoken sets the range everyone then argues around. Ask for the consequence before anyone offers a score, and take the score last.
The highest-paid person’s opinion quietly becomes the room’s opinion. The finding stops being the group’s assessment and turns into theirs, unchallenged.
One confident owner crowds out three quieter ones who sit closer to the work. Airtime is not evidence; redistributing it is the facilitator’s job.
The room slides into solutioning — designing the fix — before the risks are even listed. Park every proposed control on a separate sheet and go back to naming risks.

blocks.html:
The tendency for the first figure said aloud to fix the range every later
estimate clusters around. In a workshop it is countered by scoring last, after
the cause and consequence are agreed.

blocks.text: Turning a workshop into register entries

blocks.html: A workshop whose output never reaches the register was a meeting. Every risk should leave the room as three things: a statement with a cause, an event and a consequence; a single named owner; and a provisional score that can be revised later. The facilitator’s real task is conversion — turning an hour of argument into rows that land in the register at 3.1. Talk that is not written down as a row is talk that did not happen.

items.q: Who should attend a risk workshop?
items.html: The people who own the work and one facilitator who does not. First-line process owners supply where it breaks; a second-line facilitator keeps the session honest and converts the talk into register rows. Keep it to six to ten so everyone speaks. A room too senior will not contradict itself, and a room too junior cannot commit to a treatment.

items.q: How long should a risk workshop be?
items.html: Ninety minutes is usually the ceiling for useful attention. Past that the scoring gets careless and the quieter owners stop contributing. Cover fewer risks properly rather than the whole register badly — a second session beats one long one.

items.q: How do you stop groupthink in a risk workshop?
items.html: Take the scores last, after the cause and consequence are agreed, so the first figure said aloud cannot anchor the rest, and have the most senior person speak after the others rather than first. Then invite the disagreement explicitly. A workshop in which nobody contradicts anybody has told you nothing you did not already know.

blocks.html: Facilitating the room — holding anchoring and the loudest voice in check, not just working through the agenda — is practised in GRC Mastery’s foundation track. This entry stays free.

sections.text: Compliance is not the same as being safe

blocks.html:
Compliance knows which obligations bind the organisation, maps each one to a
control, and keeps the proof that the control ran. Three verbs, four artefacts.

The distinguishing artefact is the mapping. Without it a company running two frameworks does the same work twice and produces two control inventories that disagree — which is worse than either alone, because now nobody knows which one an auditor will be shown.

items.html: Every requirement that binds you, with its source cited — the law, the clause, the contract, the standard. An obligation with no citation cannot be tested and will not survive challenge.
What you actually do, each control mapped to the obligations it satisfies. See 4.1.
The dated proof that each control operated, retrievable by control and by period. See 4.2.
The process for receiving a request, producing the evidence, and managing what comes back. See 4.3.

blocks.html:
Four sources, and programmes routinely forget the third and fourth.

Law and regulation, which is the one everybody starts with. Contracts — customer agreements with security schedules, supplier terms, insurance conditions. Standards the organisation has voluntarily committed to, which bind in practice once a certificate is on the website. And internal policy, which binds because you wrote it down and told people to follow it.

The contractual set is usually the largest and the least catalogued. A company with two hundred customer contracts has agreed to a lot of specific things and frequently cannot list them.

One quarterly access review can satisfy an ISO 27001 Annex A control, a SOC 2 criterion, a customer contractual clause and an internal policy — with the same evidence, produced once.

That only happens if something records the relationship. An inventory with no mapping column is a to-do list; the mapping is what turns a control programme into a compliance programme.

A requirement binding the organisation, from law, contract, standard or its own
policy, recorded with the source that creates it.

blocks.text: Compliance is not the same as being safe

blocks.html:
Worth stating plainly, because the conflation causes real harm in both directions. A compliant organisation has met a defined set of obligations. Those obligations were written by somebody else, against a general case, at a point in the past.

They are a floor. The risk function exists to find what the floor does not cover, and a compliance programme that has quietly replaced the risk register with a control checklist has removed the only part of the function that was looking at your specific situation.

sections.text: Building it without losing a month

blocks.html:
A mapping records which controls satisfy which obligations. It is the artefact
that makes a second framework cost a fraction of the first, and the one most
programmes build last and regret.

The relationship is many-to-many in both directions. One control commonly satisfies six obligations; one obligation commonly needs three controls. Any model that assumes otherwise produces a mapping that has to be rebuilt.

items.html: Stable, and not the framework’s. Borrow ISO’s A.5.15 as your control ID and you will renumber the whole inventory when you add SOC 2.
What is done, in the present tense, specific enough to test. “Access is reviewed” is not testable; “privileged access to production is reviewed quarterly by the system owner” is.
The named person who operates it. Distinct from the risk owner.
How often it runs, which determines how many evidence instances an auditor will expect.
The list, with citations. This is the mapping.
What the control produces, and where it lands.

blocks.text: Building it without losing a month

blocks.html:
Start from the controls, not the frameworks. List what the organisation already does — the access review, the change approval, the backup test, the onboarding checklist — and write each as a testable statement with an owner.

Then take the framework you have been asked for and walk its requirements against that list. Three things fall out: controls that map cleanly, controls you have that nothing requires, and requirements nothing covers. The third list is your gap analysis, and it arrives as a by-product rather than as a separate six-week exercise.

Adding the second framework then takes days rather than months, because you are walking a second requirement set against an inventory that already exists.

Mapping to the framework’s structure. If your inventory is organised as Annex A, then SOC 2 has to be bolted on sideways, and NIST CSF cannot be expressed at all. Organise by what you do; map outward.

One-to-one mapping. Filling every requirement with exactly one control produces controls invented to satisfy a requirement rather than to manage a risk — and an inventory full of controls nobody runs. Some requirements are satisfied by three controls; some by a documented justification for exclusion.

A different control accepted as meeting an obligation the prescribed control
would have met, with a documented rationale. Legitimate, and audited harder than
the original.

The mapping decays at every framework revision and every reorganisation. Two habits keep it alive: review it when a control owner changes rather than annually, and treat a new customer contract clause as an obligation-register event rather than a legal one.

The second is the one that catches programmes out. A security schedule agreed by the sales team in March is an obligation from March, and the first anybody in compliance hears of it is usually the audit.

entries.title: Evidence that holds up in audit
entries.description: Audit-grade evidence is dated, attributable, complete for the period, and intelligible to someone who was not there. The four properties, and the screenshot habits that fail all of them.
sources: IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 2310 (Identifying Information)

sections.text: What to keep, and for how long

blocks.html:
Evidence is a dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient
for a reviewer who was not present to conclude that the control ran as
described. Everything else is documentation.
The gap between “we do this” and “we can show we did this” is where most first audits are lost, and it is almost never because the control was not running.

items.html: The record shows when the control ran, in a way the system produced rather than a person typed. A screenshot with no visible timestamp establishes nothing about when.
It is clear who performed the action and who reviewed it. A shared account performing a control makes attribution impossible and usually makes the control itself a finding.
An auditor testing a quarterly control over a year expects four instances, not the best one. Evidence for three of four quarters is a gap, not a near miss.
A stranger can tell from the artefact what happened. If it needs a colleague to narrate it, the auditor records it as unsupported.

blocks.html: Completeness is the one that fails most often, and it fails quietly — a programme collects excellent evidence for the months someone remembered.

Screenshots are accepted evidence and are also the weakest common form. Cropped to hide the URL, taken after the fact, showing a filtered view with the filter out of frame, undated because the clock was outside the capture area.

Where a system can export, export. A CSV of the entitlement review with the generation timestamp in it beats twelve screenshots, is faster to produce, and cannot be accused of selection.

Where only a screenshot is possible, capture the whole window — URL bar, system clock, the account signed in, and the filter state.

blocks.text: What to keep, and for how long

blocks.html: Keep the artefact, the control it evidences, and the period it covers, linked so that any one of the three retrieves the others. The retention floor is the audit period plus one year, because the following year’s audit will sample the prior period to test consistency. Contracts and regulations frequently demand longer.

Testing a subset of a control’s instances to conclude on the whole population.
The auditor selects the sample, which is why evidence must be complete rather
than representative.

Collect at the point of operation, not at the point of request. A control that files its own evidence — the review tool exporting on completion, the ticket closing with the export attached — takes minutes once and survives audit. Evidence gathered in the four weeks before fieldwork takes the whole four weeks and still has holes in it.

sections.text: What to do when the evidence is not there
Handling a finding you disagree with
The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
An audit is a sampling exercise. The auditor selects which instances of a
control they want to see, you produce them, and the quality of the programme
shows in how few surprises that produces.
The single most useful thing to understand going in: you do not choose the sample. A programme that has collected its best evidence rather than all of it discovers this in week one of fieldwork.

Planning. Scope, period, control list, timetable. This is the moment to correct a misunderstanding about scope, and the last cheap moment to do it.

Fieldwork. Requests arrive, usually in batches, usually with a turnaround of a few days each. Someone must own the queue. Two to four weeks for a first external audit.

Findings. Draft findings come with a right of reply. Read the wording closely — the difference between “the control was not operating” and “evidence of operation was not retained” is large and often negotiable on fact.

Response and closure. Management response, remediation plan, dates. Then either closure or carry-forward to the next cycle.

blocks.text: What to do when the evidence is not there

blocks.html:
Say so, immediately, in writing.

The instinct is to reconstruct — regenerate the report today and present it as though it were produced in March. Auditors are extremely good at spotting this, it converts a control finding into an integrity finding, and integrity findings follow a programme for years.

The right move is to state that the instance is missing, say why, say what has changed so the next period is complete, and let it be a finding. A programme that self-reports a gap is treated very differently from one caught concealing the same gap.

blocks.text: Handling a finding you disagree with

blocks.html:
Two kinds of disagreement, handled differently.

Factual — the auditor has the control wrong, or has tested the wrong system. Answer with evidence, not argument, and expect it to be resolved.

Judgement — you both agree what happened and disagree about severity. This is what the management response is for. Say what you accept, say what you dispute and why, and record it. You will not usually win, and the record still matters: it is the thing you point at next year when the same finding is raised against a control you deliberately chose not to change.

Testing a subset of a control’s instances to conclude on the whole population.
Because the auditor selects the sample, evidence must be complete rather than
representative.

blocks.text: The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
Run one internally, first, on a handful of controls, with someone who did not operate them pulling the evidence. It takes two days, finds most of what the real audit would find, and moves the discovery from fieldwork to a quiet Tuesday.

Programmes that do this describe audits as administrative. Programmes that do not describe them as the worst month of the year, and both are accurate.

entries.title: The management assertion
entries.description: In a SOC 2 attestation, management, not the auditor, writes the assertion that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed.

sections.text: The assertion is management's, the opinion is the auditor's
Where ISO 27001 puts the same accountability

blocks.html: In an attestation engagement such as SOC 2, management provides a written assertion: its own statement that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed. The practitioner then opines on that assertion — the words are management’s, not the auditor’s.

For a Type II the assertion reaches further: it states that those controls operated effectively across the whole reporting period, not merely that they were well designed on one day. The report is built on top of this statement. The practitioner’s opinion is a conclusion about management’s assertion, so a weak or overstated assertion is management’s exposure and does not transfer to the firm that examined it.

blocks.text: The assertion is management's, the opinion is the auditor's

blocks.html:
These are two separate statements by two separate parties, and running them together is the most common misreading of a SOC 2 report. The assertion comes first: management describes the system and states that the description is fair and the controls suitably designed. The opinion is written on top of it — the practitioner tests, then concludes on whether management’s assertion is fairly stated. Under SSAE 18, AT-C section 205, the examination is of a subject matter for which the responsible party has made an assertion; without that assertion there is nothing for the practitioner to report on.

Aspect The assertion The opinion
Written by Management The practitioner, a licensed CPA firm
States The description is fair and controls were suitably designed Whether that assertion is fairly stated, on the evidence tested
Order Comes first Built on the assertion
Carries the exposure Management owns it The firm answers for its own testing

items.html: The system description matches the system that actually ran — its boundaries, the services in scope and the controls in place. Overstate the boundary and the assertion is signed over a system that does not exist.
The controls, as designed, would meet the applicable Trust Services Criteria if they operated as described. This, together with fair presentation, is the whole of a Type I.
For a Type II, that the controls operated effectively throughout the stated period. This is the part the practitioner tests against a sample.

Which criteria each half is measured against. The description is assessed for fair presentation against the description criteria (DC section 200); the controls are assessed against the Trust Services Criteria. Naming both keeps the report from being read against the wrong bar.

blocks.html:
A Type I assertion covers the fair presentation of the system description and the
suitability of control design at a point in time; a Type II adds that those
controls operated effectively across a period. The same Type I / Type II split is
used for SOC 1 reports.

blocks.text: Where ISO 27001 puts the same accountability

blocks.html: ISO/IEC 27001 has no direct equivalent. Certification produces a certificate from an accredited body, not an opinion on a statement management signed. The accountability lives in different machinery: clause 9.3 requires top management to review the information security management system at planned intervals, and the Statement of Applicability records which controls apply and the justification for including or excluding each. Both put a management decision on record. Neither is a signed assertion a practitioner then opines on, so an ISO certificate should never be described as resting on a management assertion.

Scope overstated. The description claims systems, locations or services the controls do not actually cover, and management signs it anyway. When the sample reaches the part that was never really in scope, the gap is management’s — it asserted something untrue.

Effectiveness the evidence cannot support. Management asserts that controls operated throughout the period when the evidence covers only part of it. A Type II assertion is that the controls operated effectively across the whole period, in all material respects — not a claim resting only on the instances that happened to be captured.

Treated as boilerplate. The assertion is read as text the auditor drafted and management merely countersigned. It is the opposite: the statement management owns and the document the whole report is built to opine on. A programme that lets the firm word its assertion has misunderstood who is exposed.

items.q: What is the difference between the management assertion and the auditor's opinion?
items.html: The assertion is management’s statement; the opinion is the practitioner’s conclusion about that statement. Management writes the assertion first — that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed, and for a Type II operated effectively over the period. The CPA firm then tests and issues an opinion on whether the assertion is fairly stated. One is the claim, the other is the verdict on the claim, and they are written by different parties.

items.q: Who signs the management assertion?
items.html: A member of management with authority over the system in scope — commonly an executive such as the chief executive, chief technology officer or head of security, depending on who owns the system description. It is signed by the organisation being examined, never by the audit firm. The signature is the point: it records that management, not the practitioner, stands behind the description and the controls.

items.q: Is there a management assertion in an ISO 27001 audit?
items.html: Not in the SOC 2 sense. ISO/IEC 27001 certification produces a certificate from an accredited body rather than an opinion on a signed statement. The nearest accountability sits in the management review required by clause 9.3 and in the Statement of Applicability, both of which record management decisions — but neither is a written assertion the auditor opines on.

entries.title: Change management as a control
entries.description: Change management is the control that changes to production are authorised, tested and documented before release. The record it leaves, and how it fails.

blocks.html: Change management is the control that changes to production are authorised, tested and documented before release — so no change reaches a live system without a record of who asked, who approved, what was tested and when it went out.

An unauthorised change to production is a common way a control that looks healthy on paper turns out not to be operating. It is also among the first things an auditor tests, because a weak change process quietly undermines every other control: each of them assumes that production only changes through a path someone approved.

The value of the control is not the paperwork. It is that the paperwork cannot be produced honestly after the fact, so a change is either evidenced as authorised or it is unsupported — and to an auditor an authorisation that cannot be evidenced is one that did not happen.
A valid change leaves a single record that links four things, each attributable to a named person and each dated by the system rather than typed in afterwards.

items.html: What is being changed and why, raised before the work starts. A request opened after deployment is not a request; it is a reconstruction.
A named approver who is not the person who built the change, recorded before release. This is the authorisation the whole control exists to capture.
Evidence that the change was exercised before it reached production — the test that ran, its outcome and where it ran. “Tested: yes” is not a test result.
When the change went live, who released it and to which system. This is the line that ties the approved change to the thing now running.

blocks.html: Read as a chain, the record answers request, approval, test then deployment for every change, and an auditor sampling releases reads it in that order. A change missing any link is the link the finding names.

The person who builds a change must not be the sole approver and deployer of it. A change approved by its own author records an authorisation that never happened: there was no second judgement, only a signature the requester wrote for themselves. The issue is segregation of duties, not which line reviews — a second reviewer in the same first line is fine; the author signing for themselves is not.

Segregation here is not bureaucracy. It is the difference between a control that catches a bad or malicious change before release and one that only documents it afterwards. The approver need not be senior; they need to be someone other than the author, with enough context to refuse.

ITIL 4 and many control frameworks sort changes into three paths, and the point of the split is to match the weight of the process to the risk of the change rather than force everything through one gate.

Type Path Approval Review
Normal Assessed and approved through the standard route Before release, by someone other than the author At release
Standard Pre-authorised, low-risk and repeatable Granted once, to the change type On the pre-authorisation, periodically
Emergency Expedited for genuine urgency Compressed, by an emergency approver Retrospective, and mandatory

The boundaries — what counts as low-risk, how fast an emergency has to be — are the organisation’s own to set; the three-way split is the part that travels. The emergency path exists for real incidents where waiting for normal approval would do more harm than the change. Authorisation is compressed — an emergency approver signs quickly — not removed; deferring approval to a retrospective review is an exceptional contingency, not the design. It is also the one most often abused, because it is the fastest route through the gate.

Four failure modes account for most change-management findings, and a tester who knows them looks for them first.

The emergency back door. When a large share of changes come through the emergency path, the path has stopped being for emergencies. It has become the route the organisation uses to skip approval, and a rate — emergency changes as a proportion of all changes — is the single most revealing number in the process.

Approver equals requester. The record shows an approval, but the approver and the requester are the same person, or the same shared account. There is a signature and no authorisation. This is the failure segregation exists to prevent, and it survives in programmes that check the box for “approved” without checking who approved.

“Tested” with no test. The change record asserts the change was tested and carries nothing that shows a test ran — no result, no environment, no output. An assertion of testing is not evidence of testing, and an auditor treats the two very differently.

Standing approvals. A blanket or standing approval authorises a category of change rather than a change, so everything inside the category ships without a fresh decision. Standard changes are the bounded, reviewed version of this; a standing approval that is really an open door is not.

Each of these is a control deviation before anyone has named it. When a tester samples releases and finds one that reached production with no approval on file, or an approval signed by its own author, that is the deviation the report records — and the emergency queue is a place testers commonly look first.

A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a reviewer
who was not present to conclude that the control ran. A change record is
evidence in exactly this sense, which is why “tested: yes” with nothing behind
it fails.

items.q: What is a change management control?
items.html: It is the control that a change to production is authorised, tested and documented before it is released, so that no change reaches a live system without a record of who requested it, who approved it, what was tested and when it went out. ISO/IEC 27001’s Annex A control 8.32 and the Trust Services criterion CC8.1 both frame it this way. The control is operating when that record exists for every change and the approver is never the author.

items.q: What is an emergency change?
items.html: An emergency change is one released through an expedited path because genuine urgency — an active incident, a live outage — makes waiting for normal approval more harmful than the change itself. Authorisation is expedited — compressed to an emergency approver, and only exceptionally deferred to a mandatory retrospective review. The path is legitimate and necessary; it is also the one most often abused, so the proportion of changes that use it is worth watching.

items.q: What evidence does an auditor want for change management?
items.html: The change record: the request, the approval by someone other than the requester, the test result and the deployment, each attributable to a named person and dated by the system. For a sample of changes across the whole period, not the best one. A change with a missing approval, an approval by its own author or a “tested” flag with no test behind it is recorded as a deviation.
