entries.title: Backup and restore testing
entries.description: The control is the proven restore, not the existence of a backup. What a real restore test involves, and the failure modes an untested backup hides.
sources: AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (criteria A1.2 and A1.3)
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

sections.text: What the restore has to prove
What a real restore test involves

blocks.html: The control is the restore test, not the existence of a backup — an untested backup is an assumption, and the only proof a backup works is a restore that produced usable data inside the required time.

A backup that has never been restored is a cost with an unproven benefit. It occupies storage, sits on the control list and reassures nobody who has actually needed one, because the ways a backup fails live almost entirely on the restore side — media that cannot be read, a key nobody kept, a set that was always missing a table. None of those show up while the backup job is the only thing anyone watches.

This is why an auditor testing information backup under ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control 8.13 — which requires backup copies to be maintained and regularly tested — or recovery under Trust Services criterion A1.3, asks to see a restore that happened rather than a backup schedule that runs. The schedule is the assumption; the restore is the evidence.

blocks.text: What the restore has to prove

blocks.html: A restore test is where the recovery point objective and recovery time objective stop being aspirations. The business impact analysis sets both — how much data the organisation can afford to lose (the RPO) and how long it can afford to be without the activity (the RTO) — and those numbers are derived from the impact of the outage, not picked by whoever runs the backup tool. A restore either returns data recent enough to meet the RPO, within the restore-time budget the RTO allows, or it does not. The full activity recovery time is proven by an end-to-end recovery exercise — of which the data restore is one part; see business continuity at 3.6. Nothing short of an actual restore tells you whether the data half will hold.

The maximum tolerable data loss, expressed as a length of time rather than a
volume — the point in the past back to which data must be recoverable. A restore
that returns data older than the RPO has failed even if every file it produces
opens cleanly.

blocks.text: What a real restore test involves

blocks.html:
A real restore test recovers the data into a clean, separate environment — never over the top of live production and never back into the system that just failed — and then someone confirms the recovered data is complete and usable. Usable means opened, queried and reconciled against a known record; a job that reports success has told you it finished writing, not that what it wrote can be read back. The restore is timed, from start to usable, and that figure is measured against the RTO. Then the result is documented — what was restored, from which copy, how long it took, what was checked — so the next audit reads a record instead of a memory.

A full restore recovers everything; a sampled restore recovers a defined subset. Sampling is legitimate and often the only affordable way to test often, but the sample has to exercise the real path — the same media, the same decryption, the same sequence — or it proves only that the easy part works.

Dimension Full restore Sampled restore
Scope The whole dataset or system A defined subset of files or records
Proves The recovery path end to end The path works for what was sampled
Cost Time, and a full-size clean environment Cheaper and faster, so run more often
The trap Rare, so the RTO stays untested between runs A sample that skips the hard parts proves nothing

Every one of these passes the backup dashboard.

Green for years, then nothing to restore. The jobs report success for so long that no one questions them, and the first real restore meets missing media, a decryption key nobody held or a set that turns out to have never been complete. The dashboard measured that the job ran, not that its output could be recovered.

Testing the flag, not the restore. The “test” checks that the backup job finished with a success code instead of performing an actual restore. This proves the software can write a file. It says nothing about whether that file reconstructs into working data.

Restoring into the same failure. The restore is run back into the environment that failed, reusing its configuration, its keys and its dependencies. It works, and proves nothing about recovering when that environment is the thing that is gone — which is the scenario a backup exists for.

Works in the lab, never timed. The restore succeeds but was never run against the clock, so the RTO is a number in a plan that no exercise has ever met. A recovery time nobody has measured is a guess, and it is usually optimistic.

items.q: What is the difference between a backup and a restore test?
items.html: A backup is the copy; a restore test is the proof the copy is worth keeping. The backup is made by a scheduled job and confirmed by that job reporting success — which only means data was written somewhere. The restore test reads that data back into a separate environment and confirms it reconstructs into something complete, usable and recent enough to meet the RPO. One is an activity that runs; the other is the control that shows the activity was worth running.

items.q: How often should you test restores?
items.html: Often enough that the gap between two tests is shorter than the time it would take a silent failure to matter, and always after a material change to the system, the backup method or the encryption. A yearly full restore with lighter sampled restores in between is a common shape, and higher-tier systems are tested more often — but those figures are examples, not a rule from any standard. The real cadence follows the criticality set in the BIA and the rate at which the environment changes; a system that was re-platformed last month should not be relying on a restore proven against the old one.

items.q: What does a restore test prove?
items.html: That a specific backup, restored by a specific path, produced data that was complete, usable and recent enough to meet the RPO, within the restore time the RTO budget allows — on the day it was run. Proving the full activity recovery time still needs an end-to-end exercise; a data restore is one part of it. It does not prove the next restore will succeed, which is why the test is repeated and why its result is documented each time. A single successful restore retires the assumption for one configuration; it does not retire it forever.

entries.title: Control deviations and exceptions in testing
entries.description: A control deviation is a tested instance where a control did not operate as designed — what a SOC 2 report calls an exception, and why it is not a waiver.
sources: IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 2320

sections.text: A deviation is not a waiver
What one deviation says about the population

blocks.html: A control deviation is an instance in the tested sample where the control did not operate as designed — in a SOC 2 report these are called exceptions, and a single one can put the whole control’s conclusion in question.

A deviation is a finding about the control, not about the one instance that failed. The auditor never sees the whole population — they test a sample and conclude back to everything that sample stands for — so a deviation bears on the conclusion for the whole population, not just the one instance that failed. How you treat it, more than the deviation itself, is what the auditor watches next.

blocks.text: A deviation is not a waiver

blocks.html:
The two get confused because both describe a control that was not met, and the confusion is expensive. A policy waiver is a decision made before the fact: a named approver signs off, in advance, that a specific gap will run for a bounded period with a compensating control. A deviation is a failure discovered after the fact, in testing, that nobody authorised.

Recasting a deviation as a waiver once the auditor has found it is the move that turns a control finding into an integrity finding. Back-dating an approval to cover an instance that already failed is not exception management; it is fabricated evidence, and it follows a programme far longer than the deviation ever would.

A planned, pre-authorised and time-bound exception, signed before the gap opens
and paired with a compensating control. A deviation is the opposite in every
respect: unplanned, unauthorised and found only after the control has already
failed.

blocks.text: What one deviation says about the population

blocks.html:
The auditor tests a sample — say 25 change tickets out of a year’s several thousand — and concludes on the whole population from it. One deviation in that sample of 25 is not one late change to be corrected in place; it puts the operating-effectiveness conclusion for every change the sample stood for in question, and commonly prompts the auditor to expand testing to see how far it reaches. The figures here are illustrative, and this sampling is judgemental rather than statistical, so it supports a conclusion about the population, not a precise failure rate — estimating an actual rate would need a valid probability sample.

This is why “we fixed the ticket” is the wrong instinct. Correcting the sampled instance leaves the population — and the conclusion the sample was testing — exactly where they were.
The question that decides the response is whether the deviation is a one-off or the visible edge of a control that does not work.

items.html: A single instance failed for a reason that does not recur — a one-time manual slip, a cycle with the reviewer on leave and no cover. The design holds; one operation of it did not.

The deviation reflects a design or operating failure that will recur — the control has no step that would have caught the case, or the step exists and is routinely skipped. Every untested instance is now suspect.

blocks.html: Root cause is what tells the two apart, and you cannot assert “isolated” without having found one. A deviation labelled isolated with no analysis behind it reads to an auditor as systematic with the analysis skipped.

A response answers why the control failed and what changes because of it; it does not argue that the failure should not have counted. Three parts carry it.

Root cause. Why the instance failed, established by analysis rather than assumed. Until it is known, isolated versus systematic cannot be answered and the remediation is a guess.

Remediation. What changes so the failure does not recur, across the population and not only for the sampled instance. A fix that touches one ticket and leaves the process untouched has remediated nothing.

A statement of what failed. Whether the control’s design was inadequate or a sound design was not operated. The two lead to different fixes, and an honest answer to which it was is worth more than any argument that the deviation should not count.

Four moves recur, and each one makes the finding worse.

Arguing it away. Spending the response explaining why the deviation does not really count instead of finding why it happened. The auditor has already recorded it; the only open question is the cause, and the effort spent on the argument is the effort that would have shrunk the finding.

Back-dating a waiver. Producing an approval, dated before the failure, to reclassify a deviation as a planned exception. This converts a routine control finding into an integrity finding and is the most damaging response available.

Assuming one means one. Treating a single exception in a small sample as a single isolated problem. One deviation in a sample of 25 speaks to the whole population the sample stood for, and because the sample is small and judgemental it rarely proves the problem is contained to the instance that failed.

Fixing the instance, not the population. Remediating the sampled item and leaving every other instance as it was. The sample stood for the population; the response has to reach the same population.

items.q: What is a control deviation?
items.html: A control deviation is an instance, found while testing a control, where the control did not operate as it was designed to. In SOC 2 and other examination reports these are called exceptions. Because the auditor tests a sample and concludes on the whole population, a deviation bears on whether the control operated effectively across everything the sample stood for, not just the instance that failed — so it is not a single fault to be corrected in place.

items.q: What is the difference between a deviation and a policy exception?
items.html: Timing and authorisation. A policy exception, or waiver, is planned: a named approver signs off in advance that a specific gap will run for a bounded period, with a compensating control. A deviation is unplanned: a failure discovered after the fact, in testing, that nobody authorised. Reclassifying a deviation as an exception once an auditor has found it — by back-dating the approval — turns a control finding into an integrity finding.

items.q: Does one exception fail a SOC 2 control?
items.html: Not automatically. A single exception does not by itself mean the criterion was not met; the service auditor evaluates the cause of the exception, whether it is isolated or systematic and what it implies for the rest of the population before concluding. One exception can contribute to a qualified opinion when its effect is material, and it can also be judged isolated and immaterial — which is why the root cause and the response matter more than the count.

entries.title: Continuous control monitoring
entries.description: Continuous control monitoring is automated, ongoing proof that a control is operating, taken from the system itself instead of screenshotted once a quarter.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation)
NIST SP 800-137 — Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)

sections.text: What automation suits, and what it does not
What it feeds, and what it does not replace

blocks.html: Continuous control monitoring is automated, ongoing checking that a control is operating, pulling the signal straight from the system rather than screenshotting it once a quarter. Continuous compliance is the broader goal it feeds — staying provably within requirements over time — which takes acting on what the monitoring finds, not watching alone.

It closes the gap between “we do this” and “we can show we did this” to near zero for the controls it covers, because the evidence 4.2 is produced at the moment the control operates rather than gathered in the four weeks before fieldwork. What it cannot do is exercise judgement, so it earns its place on the controls a machine can check and leaves the rest exactly where they were.

Point-in-time evidence answers one question: did the control run on the day someone looked. Continuous control monitoring answers a harder one: has it run every day since, and can you see the moment it stopped. The record is pulled at the point of operation, continuously, from the system that enforces the control rather than assembled by hand before an audit.

That is the whole value. Evidence 4.2 collected this way is dated and attributable by construction, and complete for the period its coverage actually spans — provided the monitoring itself has no gaps and its telemetry can be trusted. The programme stops sampling its own best month and starts holding the full population it covers.

blocks.text: What automation suits, and what it does not

blocks.html:
Automation suits a control whose correct state a machine can read without interpretation. It does not suit a control whose correctness is a person’s judgement, and wiring one of those to a green tick produces a light with no thought behind it.

Suits continuous monitoring Does not
MFA coverage across privileged accounts A manager’s review of an exception
Encryption configuration on a data store A risk-acceptance decision
Access still matching the joiner-mover-leaver record Whether a vendor is trustworthy
Patch currency against a baseline Whether a policy is the right policy

The left column is machine-checkable: there is a correct state and the system can report the current one against it. The right column is not. A tool can confirm that a review was recorded; it cannot confirm the review was any good, and treating the record of a judgement as the judgement itself is how a green dashboard hides a hollow control.

blocks.text: What it feeds, and what it does not replace

blocks.html: A continuously monitored control is a natural source for a leading indicator. Coverage trending down — privileged accounts without a second factor creeping from two per cent to four — is an early warning while there is still time to act, not a surprise discovered at quarter end.

A leading metric that warns exposure is moving toward appetite before it becomes
an incident. A continuously monitored control is one of the cleanest feeds for
one, because the coverage figure updates itself.

It does not replace the audit. An auditor still tests, still selects the sample and still concludes independently — but tests against a population that is already instrumented, where the evidence exists for every instance rather than the ones that were remembered. Continuous monitoring makes fieldwork shorter and duller. It does not make it unnecessary, and a programme that treats a platform’s green dashboard as an audit opinion has confused the two.

Watching the tool, not the control. A monitor that confirms the scanner is online says nothing about whether the scan is finding anything. The signal has to be the operation of the control, not the availability of the thing that checks it.

Alerting on everything. A monitor that fires on every deviation, at any severity, trains everyone to ignore it. Within a month the alerts are a filtered folder and a real breach sits in it unread. Thresholds and routing are part of the design, not an afterthought.

“Continuous” that is really monthly. A check that runs on a schedule slow enough to miss the thing it watches is point-in-time sampling with a dashboard. If a control can drift and be restored between runs, the gap is invisible and the word is marketing.

Coverage mistaken for effectiveness. Buying a compliance-automation platform and counting the controls it touches measures reach, not operation. A control can be monitored, green and not working; coverage is the count of controls watched, effectiveness is whether the watched control does its job.

items.q: What is continuous control monitoring?
items.html: It is automated, ongoing checking that a control is operating, taken from the system that runs the control rather than reconstructed by hand before an audit. Instead of confirming a control worked on the day someone screenshotted it, it confirms the control has stayed in its required state and shows the moment it did not. It suits controls with a machine-checkable state — MFA coverage, encryption settings, patch currency 4.10 — and is poorly suited to controls that turn on human judgement.

items.q: What is the difference between continuous monitoring and continuous compliance?
items.html: Continuous monitoring is one activity inside continuous compliance, not the whole of it. Monitoring reads a control’s condition on an ongoing basis. Continuous compliance is the broader practice of staying provably within requirements over time — which takes evaluating what the monitoring surfaces and remediating what it finds, not monitoring alone. Monitoring makes the state visible; holding it is more than watching.

items.q: Can continuous monitoring replace an audit?
items.html: No. It feeds an audit rather than removing the need for one. An auditor still selects a sample, tests independently and forms an opinion, but does it against a population that is already instrumented, so fieldwork is shorter and holds fewer surprises. A platform’s green dashboard is evidence for an audit, not a substitute for the auditor’s own testing.

entries.title: Security questionnaires (SIG, CAIQ)
entries.description: A security questionnaire is a standardised set of questions used to assess a vendor's security posture. The SIG and CAIQ are the common templates.
sources: Shared Assessments, Standardized Information Gathering (SIG) Questionnaire
Cloud Security Alliance, Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ) and STAR
ISO/IEC 27036-2:2022 — Cybersecurity, supplier relationships, Part 2: Requirements

sections.text: Why a completed questionnaire is not assurance
Tier the questionnaire to the risk

blocks.html: A security questionnaire is a standardised set of questions used to assess a vendor’s security posture — the SIG and the CAIQ are the common templates — and it is a diligence artefact, not assurance in itself.

The questionnaire is where third-party diligence usually starts, and it is where weak programmes stop. Treating the returned document as the assessment confuses the instrument for the finding: three hundred answered questions with nothing sampled behind them tell you what a vendor is willing to assert, not what is true.

The same document sits on two desks, and most people only ever meet one side of it.

Sending. As part of third-party diligence, the questionnaire goes out to a prospective or existing vendor to probe its security posture before and during the relationship. It is one instrument of the wider vendor due diligence at 3.8, not the whole of it — a completed questionnaire narrows what still needs verifying, it does not close the assessment.

Answering. As the vendor being assessed, you complete other organisations’ questionnaires to win and keep their business. For a company that sells to enterprises this is a standing workload measured in hundreds of questions a quarter, and it turns into a revenue-blocking task the moment a deal waits on it.

blocks.text: Why a completed questionnaire is not assurance

blocks.html:
The answers are self-attested. A vendor asserting that access is reviewed quarterly and data is encrypted at rest has told you what it believes to be true; it has shown you nothing. Assurance arrives only with the artefact behind the answer — an independent audit report such as SOC 2, an ISO 27001 certificate scoped to the service you are buying or an actual configuration export.

A “yes” with nothing behind it is a claim, not a control. A SOC 2 report and an ISO 27001 certificate answer different questions — see 5.1 — and a certificate scoped to the wrong entity proves nothing about the service in front of you. The questionnaire tells you what to verify; the evidence is what verifies it.

blocks.text: Tier the questionnaire to the risk

blocks.html:
Sending a three-hundred-question SIG to a vendor that stores none of your data and touches none of your systems is questionnaire theatre: it burns the vendor’s time and yours, and nobody reads the result. Depth of questionnaire should follow the risk tier set in third-party risk management — a lightweight set for a routine supplier, the full instrument reserved for a vendor inside a recovery time objective or holding production data. The SIG ships in exactly this spirit, with a shorter SIG Lite for lower-tier suppliers and the full SIG Core for the ones that can actually hurt you.

Dimension SIG CAIQ
Author Shared Assessments Cloud Security Alliance
Scope Broad third-party risk across many control domains Cloud service security, mapped to the Cloud Controls Matrix
Form Configurable question set, from SIG Core down to SIG Lite Yes/no control assertions against CCM domains
Standing Licensed content set, maintained and updated Freely available, underpinning CSA STAR registry listings

Redrafting the same three hundred questions by hand every time is how the workload becomes unbearable and how the answers go stale. The fix is a reviewed knowledge base — every standard question with an approved answer and a link to the evidence behind it — that a response can be assembled from and then tailored to the asker.

It needs a named owner who keeps it current. An answer library nobody maintains is a catalogue of last year’s claims, and the drift is invisible until a customer’s auditor asks to see the control behind an answer that stopped being true two releases ago.

A completed questionnaire treated as assurance. The document comes back, gets filed and closes the assessment, with no report, certificate or export sampled behind a single answer. The programme has collected assertions and recorded them as facts.

Answers that drift from reality. The questionnaire is refreshed once a year while the environment changes every week. Between refreshes the answers describe a posture the organisation no longer has, and nobody notices until an incident or an audit finds the gap.

Questionnaire theatre. Hundreds of questions issued and returned, none validated. The volume signals diligence and delivers none — a longer questionnaire that nobody checks is weaker than a short one that is verified.

One questionnaire for every tier. A low-risk vendor is sent the same instrument as a critical one, so the routine supplier is over-assessed and the critical one is assessed no harder than the rest. Effort decouples from risk, and the review that mattered gets the same cursory read as the ninety that did not.

items.q: What is a security questionnaire?
items.html: A standardised set of questions an organisation sends a vendor to assess its security posture, or receives and completes when it is the vendor being assessed. The SIG and the CAIQ are the two common templates. It is a diligence artefact — a structured way to ask — and not assurance in itself, because the answers are self-attested until evidence is produced behind them.

items.q: What is the difference between a SIG and a CAIQ?
items.html: The SIG (Standardized Information Gathering, from Shared Assessments) is a broad third-party-risk questionnaire covering many control domains, licensed as a maintained content set and configurable from a full SIG Core down to a shorter SIG Lite. The CAIQ (Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire, from the Cloud Security Alliance) is narrower and cloud-specific: yes/no control assertions mapped to the Cloud Controls Matrix and freely available, and a submitted CAIQ is what backs a Level 1 listing in the CSA STAR registry. Use the SIG for general supplier diligence; expect the CAIQ from a cloud provider.

items.q: Is a completed security questionnaire enough assurance?
items.html: No. A completed questionnaire is a set of claims, not evidence they are true. Assurance comes from what stands behind the answers — an independent audit report such as SOC 2, a certification such as ISO 27001 scoped to the service in question or a direct artefact like a configuration export. Treat the questionnaire as the thing that tells you what to verify, then verify the answers that matter.

blocks.html:
The assessment of a supplier’s security, financial and regulatory standing before
and during the relationship, scaled to the risk tier. A questionnaire is one
instrument of that diligence, not the whole of it — verifying what the answers
claim is the rest.
Running a vendor questionnaire programme — tiering, an answer library and demanding evidence behind the answers — is worked through in GRC Mastery’s third-party risk module. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Vulnerability management
entries.description: The lifecycle of discovering, prioritising, remediating and verifying technical vulnerabilities on deadlines set by severity — not a one-off scan report.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.8 (management of technical vulnerabilities)
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 — Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning

sections.text: CVSS is not risk on its own
The link to KRIs and continuous monitoring

blocks.html: Vulnerability management is the lifecycle of discovering, prioritising, remediating and verifying technical vulnerabilities on time limits set by severity — a continuous programme, not a scan report filed and forgotten.

The scan is the easy part. What separates a programme from a report is everything after the finding: a decision about which vulnerabilities matter, a deadline to fix them by, and a rescan that proves each one is actually closed. A scanner that runs every week feeding a queue that never empties is not vulnerability management — it is a list that grows.

items.html: Authenticated scanning, penetration testing and vendor and disclosure feeds find what is exposed. An unauthenticated scan sees the front door; an authenticated one sees the missing patches behind it.
CVSS is the starting point, adjusted for active exploitation, exposure and asset criticality. A base score ranks the finding in the abstract; context ranks it on your estate.
Patch, or apply a mitigating control, within a time limit set by severity. The SLA is the commitment; without one the finding has no deadline and no owner.

Rescan — or authoritative version or configuration evidence — to confirm the fix closed the vulnerability rather than moved it. “Remediated” in a ticket is a claim; a clean rescan is evidence that holds up.

blocks.text: CVSS is not risk on its own

blocks.html:
A CVSS score measures the vulnerability, not the risk it poses to you. The base score is a property of the flaw — how hard it is to exploit and what it grants — computed the same way for every organisation on earth. Risk is that score meeting your estate.

Illustratively, a CVSS 9.8 on an internal host reachable only from an administrative network, sitting behind a compensating control, may matter less than a 6.5 on an internet-facing system with a public exploit in active use — the scores are examples, not thresholds. Three things sit on top of the base score and change the order: active exploitation, whether a working exploit exists and is being used; exposure, whether an attacker can reach the asset at all; and the criticality of the asset itself.

Severity then sets the clock. A programme might commit to fixing critical findings within 7 days, high within 30 and medium within 90 — but those windows are illustrative. The real ones are the organisation’s own decision, written down and agreed before the first breach rather than argued after it.

A scanner and a penetration test both discover, and neither is a substitute for the other. A scanner enumerates known weaknesses against a signature database; a test tries to exploit what it finds and chains several weaknesses into a path a scanner would report as three unrelated mediums.

Vulnerability scan Penetration test
Method Enumerates known weaknesses Exploits and chains them
Cadence Continuous or scheduled Point in time
Coverage Broad and automated Deep and targeted
Tells you What is probably wrong What an attacker could do
Blind to Anything with no signature Whatever is out of scope

A programme that runs scans and calls it testing has confirmed neither what is present nor what is exploitable.

blocks.text: The link to KRIs and continuous monitoring

blocks.html: Two other entries connect here. The count of critical vulnerabilities open past their SLA can be a key risk indicator 3.11: the SLA defines when one is overdue, and the indicator’s own threshold — how many overdue is too many — is a separate appetite decision, with a named owner and a response when it breaches. And vulnerability state — new criticals, SLA breaches and scan coverage — is a strong candidate for continuous monitoring (4.8) rather than a quarterly snapshot, because the exposure changes daily as new vulnerabilities are disclosed against software that has not moved.

A leading metric that warns exposure is moving toward appetite before it becomes
an incident. The count of critical vulnerabilities still open past their SLA is a
candidate: the SLA sets what counts as overdue, and it earns the name once it has
its own threshold, owner and response.

Scanning with no remediation SLA. The report is produced on schedule and nobody acts on it, because no deadline attaches to any line. A finding with no date is a finding no one owns.

Prioritising by CVSS base score alone. Ranking the queue by base score puts a theoretical critical on an unreachable host above a medium being exploited on the perimeter today. Strip out exploitability and exposure and the order is wrong in exactly the cases that matter.

No rescan, so “remediated” is unverified. A ticket closed on a promise is not a closed vulnerability. Patches fail to apply, roll back on reboot or fix one instance and miss four identical ones; only a rescan, or authoritative evidence of the fixed version, tells the difference.

Counting scanned assets as covered. An unauthenticated scan reaches a host but sees almost nothing installed on it. Reporting that host as assessed records coverage the scan never had, and the missing patches behind it never enter the queue.

items.q: What is vulnerability management?
items.html: Vulnerability management is the continuous lifecycle of finding technical vulnerabilities, deciding which ones matter, fixing them within a time limit set by severity and rescanning to confirm the fix held. It is a programme, not a scan: the scan is one input, and the value is in the prioritisation, the remediation SLA and the verification that follow it.

items.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
items.html: A scan enumerates known weaknesses automatically against a signature database — broad, fast and repeatable. A penetration test tries to exploit what is found and chain several weaknesses into an attack path, which a scanner cannot do. Both discover, and neither replaces the other: the scan gives coverage, the test gives depth and confirms what is genuinely exploitable.

items.q: How do you prioritise vulnerabilities?
items.html: Start from the CVSS base score, then adjust for three things it does not know: whether a working exploit exists and is being used, whether an attacker can actually reach the asset and how critical that asset is. A medium score on an exposed system under active exploitation outranks a critical on an isolated host behind a compensating control. CVSS ranks the flaw; context ranks the risk.

entries.title: How to read a framework
entries.description: Four kinds of document get called a framework, and they answer different questions. Which one you are holding determines what you can do with the output.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems, requirements
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The two questions that sort them
What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
Four different kinds of document are called frameworks, and they are not
alternatives. Which kind you are holding decides what its output is worth to
whoever asked for it.
The question “which framework should we do” is nearly always answered by who is asking and what they will accept, not by the merits of the documents.

items.html: Specifies requirements a management system must meet. An accredited body audits against it and issues a certificate. ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9001, ISO 22301.
Criteria a practitioner tests your described controls against, producing a report rather than a certificate. SOC 2 against the Trust Services Criteria.
A vocabulary and structure for describing where you are. Not a bar to clear, and nothing certifies against it. NIST CSF 2.0, with its six functions.
A model of how control and risk should reach a governing body. Used to design a programme, not to test one. COSO ERM, the IIA’s Three Lines Model.

blocks.text: The two questions that sort them

blocks.html:
What does it produce? A certificate travels and can be published. A report is read, usually under NDA, and says considerably more. A profile or a maturity score says where you are and binds you to nothing. A model produces a design.

Who audits it? An accredited certification body, a licensed practitioner, yourself, or nobody. This is what determines whether the output means anything to a third party — a self-assessed anything is worth exactly the trust already placed in you.

Three things to find before anything else.

The scope clause. Every certifiable standard has one, and it is where the real negotiation happens. A certificate covering one product line is not a certificate covering the company, and the scope statement is printed on it.

The shall/should boundary. In a standard, “shall” is a requirement and “should” is a recommendation. Auditors test the first and ask about the second. Reading a standard without noticing which is which produces a programme that gold-plates recommendations and misses requirements.

The annex’s status. ISO 27001’s Annex A is a reference control set you justify including or excluding, not a checklist you complete. Treating it as mandatory is the single most expensive misreading in the discipline.

The oversight of the certification bodies themselves, by a national
accreditation body. An unaccredited certificate is a document a company bought.

blocks.text: What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
The controls overlap heavily — access, change, vulnerabilities, incidents, vendors, backups. The shells do not: ISO wants a management system with internal audit and management review; SOC 2 wants a system description and the auditor’s own testing; NIST CSF wants neither and gives you a profile.

Budget for one control programme and as many reporting shells as you have buyers. See 5.2 for the artefact that makes that affordable.

entries.title: ISO 27001 vs SOC 2
entries.description: ISO 27001 certifies a management system and produces a certificate. SOC 2 is an attestation over control operation and produces a report. Which one your buyer is actually asking for.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Information security management systems, requirements
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022

sections.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
ISO/IEC 27001 certifies that a management system exists and works, and produces
a certificate. SOC 2 attests that specific controls operated over a period, and
produces a report someone reads. They answer different questions for different
buyers.
The question “which should we do first” is nearly always settled by who is asking for it, not by the merits of either standard.

sides.name: ISO/IEC 27001
sides.html:
An accredited body audits your ISMS against the standard and issues a
certificate you can publish. Annex A supplies a reference control set you
justify including or excluding.

sides.name: SOC 2
sides.html:
A licensed CPA firm tests the controls you describe against the Trust Services
Criteria and writes a report, usually shared under NDA. No fixed control list —
you describe your own, then prove them.

rows.b: Type I point in time; Type II a period

blocks.html: The fixed-control-list row is the structural difference and the one that surprises people. ISO 27001 hands you a reference set of controls in Annex A and asks you to justify inclusions and exclusions in a Statement of Applicability. SOC 2 hands you criteria and asks you to describe the controls you have chosen to meet them. One is a checklist you argue with; the other is an essay you must then prove.

The document recording which Annex A controls apply, which do not, and the
justification for each decision. Required by ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 d).

A distinction only SOC 2 has, and the one most often got wrong in sales conversations.

Type I says the controls were suitably designed at a point in time. It is a snapshot, achievable quickly, and a sophisticated buyer will note that it proves nothing about operation.

Type II says the controls operated effectively across a period — commonly three to twelve months. This is what enterprise procurement means when it says “SOC 2”. A first Type II usually covers a shorter window, then extends to twelve months on the next cycle.

blocks.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
The control sets overlap substantially. Access review, change management, vulnerability management, incident response, vendor management and backup do work for both, with the same evidence.

What does not transfer is the shell around them. ISO 27001 requires management system machinery — scope, policy, risk assessment methodology, internal audit, management review, corrective action — that SOC 2 has no equivalent of. SOC 2 requires a system description and a control matrix in a specific form, plus an auditor’s own testing, which ISO does not.

Budget for one control programme and two reporting shells. Organisations that budget for two programmes spend roughly twice what they need to and produce two inconsistent control inventories, which is worse than the cost.

If your buyers are North American technology companies, they will ask for SOC 2 and many will not recognise an ISO certificate. If they are European, or enterprise procurement anywhere, they will ask for ISO 27001. If they are both, do the control work once and sequence the reporting — SOC 2 Type I first for speed, ISO 27001 next for reach, SOC 2 Type II on the following cycle.
The crosswalk between Annex A and the Trust Services Criteria is built line by line in GRC Mastery’s frameworks track. This entry stays free.

entries.title: Building a control crosswalk
entries.description: A crosswalk maps one framework's requirements onto another through your own controls. How to build one that survives a revision, and why mapping framework-to-framework directly is the wrong shape.

sections.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point
What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
A crosswalk lets one control answer several frameworks at once. Built correctly
it is the reason a second certification costs a fraction of the first; built
incorrectly it is a spreadsheet that has to be thrown away at the next revision.
The critical decision is the shape. Almost every published crosswalk maps framework A directly to framework B, and almost every useful internal one maps both through your own control inventory.

blocks.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point

blocks.html:
Direct mapping produces one artefact per pair. Three frameworks means three mappings; four means six. Each is maintained separately and they drift.

Mapping through your controls means one artefact. Each control lists the requirements it satisfies across every framework you carry. Adding a fourth framework adds one column, not three documents.
The last row is where the confusion comes from. Vendors publish framework-to-framework crosswalks because they are marketable. They are a useful starting reference and a poor operating artefact.

Take the control inventory from 4.1. For each framework, walk its requirements and record against each control the requirements it satisfies. Three outputs, as always: mapped, unmapped requirements, and controls nothing requires.

Two rules keep it honest. A mapping is a claim that this control, as written, satisfies that requirement — if it only partly does, record it as partial and name the gap, because a partial mapping recorded as full is exactly what fieldwork finds. And every mapping cites the requirement identifier, not its paraphrase, so a revision can be diffed.

blocks.text: What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
ISO 27001 moved from 114 Annex A controls in 2013 to 93 in 2022, restructured into four themes. Organisations with a hub-and-spoke crosswalk re-mapped one column. Organisations with three pairwise mappings rebuilt all of them.

Assume a revision every three to five years per framework and build for it.

A control that satisfies part of a requirement, recorded with what it does not
cover. The honest form, and the one that stops a gap being discovered during
fieldwork.

For a company adding SOC 2 to an existing ISO 27001 programme, the control work is largely done and the crosswalk shows exactly which parts. What remains is the system description, the auditor’s testing, and the handful of criteria ISO does not reach.

The saving is not the certificate. It is that the second audit examines a programme that already runs, rather than a programme assembled to be examined.

entries.title: The statement of applicability
entries.description: The SoA records which ISO 27001 Annex A controls apply, which do not, and why — a decision record, not an inventory. Required by clause 6.1.3 d).

sections.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The statement of applicability records which Annex A controls apply to your
ISMS, which do not, and the justification for each decision. ISO/IEC 27001
clause 6.1.3 d) requires it, and the auditor reads it before anything else.

It is a decision record, not a control inventory. That distinction is where most first attempts go wrong: a document listing 93 controls with “implemented” beside each says nothing about why any of them applies to you.

items.html: The Annex A identifier, from the 2022 revision’s 93 controls across four themes — organisational, people, physical, technological.
Yes or no. Not “partially” — a control either applies to your scope or it does not.
Why. For an inclusion this is usually the risk it treats or the obligation it meets; for an exclusion it is why the scope does not reach it.
Whether it is in place, and where the detail lives — a pointer to your own control inventory rather than a description.

blocks.html: The justification column is the one that gets skimmed and the one that is read hardest. “Applicable — best practice” is not a justification. “Applicable — treats R-014, remote access to production” is.

Excluding a control is legitimate and expected. A company with no physical premises excludes several physical controls; a company that writes no software excludes secure development controls.

What is not legitimate is excluding a control because it is inconvenient. The justification is tested, and the obvious tell is an exclusion that contradicts the scope statement — no development controls, in a scope covering a product the company builds.

Where an exclusion is genuine, the phrasing that survives is the one that ties back to scope rather than to circumstance: not “we do not currently do this”, but “this activity is outside the ISMS scope defined in clause 4.3”.

blocks.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The SoA is the bridge between the risk assessment and the control inventory. The risk assessment says what needs treating; the SoA says which Annex A controls are in play as a result; the inventory says what you actually do and who owns it.

Keeping them as three artefacts is correct. Merging the SoA into the inventory produces a document that is neither a decision record nor an operating list, and which has to be untangled at the next audit.

The boundary of the management system, stated under clause 4.3. Everything in
the SoA is a decision made relative to it, which is why an exclusion that
contradicts scope fails immediately.

Review it whenever the scope changes, whenever the risk assessment produces a new treatment, and at the annual management review. A SoA carrying last year’s scope is the most common documentation finding in surveillance audits, and it is entirely avoidable.

entries.title: What GRC roles exist
entries.description: Analyst, manager, lead, head — plus the four specialisations the work splits into. What each seat does daily, what it pays attention to, and where each one goes next.
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

sections.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
The titles vary more than the work does. Every seat in this field is
accountable for one or more of the four artefacts, and the useful way to read a
job advert is to work out which.

Salary bands are deliberately omitted here: they move, they are regional, and a number in a reference work goes stale in a way the rest of an entry does not. What follows is what each seat actually does.

items.html: The entry seat. Runs the register day to day, chases evidence, completes customer questionnaires, keeps the policy set current. Most of the week is writing things down so somebody else can act on them.
Owns a framework end to end and the audit relationship that goes with it. First seat with a budget conversation and the first with a genuine right to say no.
Owns the register, the appetite statement and the committee reporting. Divergence point: this seat drifts toward the business, the compliance seat toward the auditors.
Owns the programme and the board narrative. Answers for the function’s opinion rather than its paperwork, and spends more time on resourcing than on controls.

blocks.html:
Third-party risk. The first split in almost every organisation, because the volume of supplier assessments is relentless and unlike the rest of the work.

Privacy. A distinct obligation set with its own regulator, its own artefacts and — where a statutory DPO is required — independence constraints that make it a poor fit for a general compliance seat.

Technology / product compliance. Sits closest to engineering. Owns the controls that live in the pipeline, and needs enough fluency to challenge an architecture decision.

Financial controls / SOX. A different lineage entirely, closer to internal audit and the finance function, with its own qualification path.

blocks.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
Not by controls implemented, in any function worth working in. Analysts are measured on whether the artefacts are current and legible. Managers on whether audits produce surprises. Heads on whether the board’s picture of risk matches the organisation’s actual position.

An interview question worth asking in the other direction: how do you know this function is working? An answer in terms of coverage percentages describes a function that reports on itself. An answer in terms of decisions made and surprises avoided describes one that is used.

The specialist functions providing expertise, challenge and monitoring to the
first line. Almost every GRC seat sits here.

Sideways more often than up, and that is normal. Risk to privacy, compliance to internal audit, GRC to security architecture, and — increasingly — GRC into product, because the person who understands the obligations understands what the product has to do.

The route out that surprises people is into consulting, where the breadth of a generalist seat is worth more than the depth of a specialist one.

entries.title: Breaking into GRC
entries.description: The field hires from IT support, audit, project delivery and law more often than from graduate schemes. What transfers, what has to be learned, and the one artefact that beats a certificate in an interview.
sources: ISACA, CRISC and CISA job practice areas, 2025

sections.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks
The thing that beats a certificate
The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Almost nobody starts here. The field hires from IT support, internal audit,
project delivery and law, and each route arrives with most of one half of the
job already done.
Knowing which half you already have is the difference between a targeted application and a scattergun one.

blocks.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks

items.html: Brings the ability to read a system you did not build and write down what happened. Lacks the evidence habit — what makes a screenshot admissible, why a date matters, what the auditor asks next.
Brings sampling, testing and the discipline of writing findings that survive challenge. Lacks the design side: this seat has never had to build the control it has spent years testing.
Brings tracking, chasing and getting a dozen people to a date. Lacks the domain — which obligations exist and why they bind.
Brings obligation reading and precision about sources. Lacks the technical literacy to challenge an engineer’s answer without accepting it whole.

blocks.text: The thing that beats a certificate

blocks.html:
One artefact you built, that you can walk somebody through end to end.

A risk you assessed: how it was raised, how you scored it and against what scale, who owned it, what treatment was chosen, who approved it, what evidence closed it. Ten minutes, specific, with the parts that went wrong included.

A candidate who can do that outperforms one with three certificates and nothing to describe, every time, because the interviewer’s actual question is whether you have handled a real artefact or only read about them.

If your current job has none, build one. Assess a risk in your own team’s work, properly, with a documented scale. It is a real artefact even if the organisation never asked for it.

They help with the screening filter and they do not close the interview.

CISA is the most widely recognised in audit-adjacent roles and does not assume a technical background. ISO 27001 Lead Implementer teaches the management-system vocabulary faster than anything else. CRISC maps well to the risk seat. A security certification like Security+ helps only if the gap you are closing is technical literacy.

Sequencing matters more than choice: a certificate taken before you have handled an artefact teaches you vocabulary with nothing to attach it to, and it fades.

blocks.text: The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Not technical depth. The evidence habit — understanding that the job is not doing the thing but being able to show, months later, to somebody who was not there, that the thing was done.

It is learnable in months and it is the thing hiring managers are listening for. Candidates who talk about what they did are common; candidates who talk about what they kept are not.
The foundation track at GRC Mastery is built around producing exactly that walk-through artefact. This entry stays free, and so does the advice: build one either way.

entries.title: Interview questions, and how to answer them
entries.description: The eight questions that come up in almost every GRC interview, what each one is really testing, and the shape of an answer that lands.

blocks.html:
Every one of these questions has a textbook answer and a real answer. The
textbook answer gets you to the next question; the real answer gets you the job.

What interviewers are testing, almost without exception, is whether you have held the artefact or only read about it. Answers that name a specific instance do that; answers that recite a definition do not.

items.q: What is the difference between GRC and internal audit?
items.html:
The accountability line, not the task list. “GRC reports to management and owns the outcome; internal audit reports to the audit committee and owns the opinion.” Everything about tools and frameworks follows from it.

The follow-up is usually about independence, and the answer they are listening for is that it is structural rather than personal — an auditor who helped fix the gap has lost the opinion they were hired to give, however honest they are. See 1.4.

items.q: Appetite or tolerance — what is the difference?
items.html:
Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives, set annually by the board, usually by category. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around one specific objective, and it is a number you can cross.

The good answer adds when the distinction bites: at the moment somebody has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted. See 3.2.

items.q: Walk me through a risk you assessed.
items.html:
The one that matters. Pick a real one, and include what went wrong.

How it was raised. How you scored it, against what documented scale. Who owned it — a person. What treatment was chosen and who had the authority to approve it. What evidence closed it. Then the honest part: what you would do differently, which is where the interview stops being a test.

items.q: How do you handle a control owner who will not give you evidence?
items.html:
They are testing whether you escalate straight away, which is the wrong answer.

Find out why first — usually the request is ambiguous, the system cannot produce what you asked for, or they do not know they own the control. Then make the request specific and easy. Escalation is the third move, not the first, and when it comes it goes with a record of the two attempts before it.

items.q: ISO 27001 or SOC 2?
items.html:
Answer with a question: who is asking for it. North American technology buyers ask for SOC 2; European and enterprise procurement asks for ISO. If both, sequence rather than choose.

Candidates who answer with a preference are describing a document they have read. Candidates who answer with the buyer are describing work they have done. See 5.1.

items.q: Is GRC a technical job?
items.html:
No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system.

Worth adding the failure mode, because it shows self-awareness: the risk is not being insufficiently technical, it is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

items.q: How would you build a programme from nothing?
items.html:
Register first, even a rough one, because the argument about the scale is easier with real entries in front of it. Then the policy set, then the control inventory with its mapping, then the evidence habit.

Starting with policy is the intuitive answer and the slow one — you end up writing rules for risks you have not established you carry. Saying so demonstrates you have thought about order rather than listing artefacts.

items.q: Where do you see the function failing?
items.html:
An invitation, and most candidates waste it on something generic about tone at the top.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between GRC and internal audit?

acceptedAnswer.text: The accountability line, not the task list. “GRC reports to management and owns the outcome; internal audit reports to the audit committee and owns the opinion.” Everything about tools and frameworks follows from it. The follow-up is usually about independence, and the answer they are listening for is that it is structural rather than personal — an auditor who helped fix the gap has lost the opinion they were hired to give, however honest they are. See 1.4 .

mainEntity.name: Appetite or tolerance — what is the difference?

acceptedAnswer.text: Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives, set annually by the board, usually by category. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around one specific objective, and it is a number you can cross. The good answer adds when the distinction bites: at the moment somebody has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted. See 3.2 .

mainEntity.name: Walk me through a risk you assessed.

acceptedAnswer.text: The one that matters. Pick a real one, and include what went wrong. How it was raised. How you scored it, against what documented scale. Who owned it — a person. What treatment was chosen and who had the authority to approve it. What evidence closed it. Then the honest part: what you would do differently, which is where the interview stops being a test.

mainEntity.name: How do you handle a control owner who will not give you evidence?

acceptedAnswer.text: They are testing whether you escalate straight away, which is the wrong answer. Find out why first — usually the request is ambiguous, the system cannot produce what you asked for, or they do not know they own the control. Then make the request specific and easy. Escalation is the third move, not the first, and when it comes it goes with a record of the two attempts before it.

mainEntity.name: ISO 27001 or SOC 2?

acceptedAnswer.text: Answer with a question: who is asking for it. North American technology buyers ask for SOC 2; European and enterprise procurement asks for ISO. If both, sequence rather than choose. Candidates who answer with a preference are describing a document they have read. Candidates who answer with the buyer are describing work they have done. See 5.1 .

mainEntity.name: Is GRC a technical job?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system. Worth adding the failure mode, because it shows self-awareness: the risk is not being insufficiently technical, it is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

mainEntity.name: How would you build a programme from nothing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Register first, even a rough one, because the argument about the scale is easier with real entries in front of it. Then the policy set, then the control inventory with its mapping, then the evidence habit. Starting with policy is the intuitive answer and the slow one — you end up writing rules for risks you have not established you carry. Saying so demonstrates you have thought about order rather than listing artefacts.

sections.text: Sequencing, which matters more than choice

blocks.html:
No single GRC certification suits every role. The right one depends on the seat
you are aiming at, how much experience you already have, and whether your
immediate need is broad grounding or specialist evidence — and most of the
respected credentials are narrower than their reputation suggests.

Almost all of the well-known certifications qualify a slice of the work rather than GRC as a whole — an audit exam, a risk exam, a management exam, a security generalist’s exam, a single standard. For someone already in a seat, that focus is the point. For someone entering the field it is the trap: a specialist credential bought before there is any context to attach it to teaches vocabulary with nothing behind it.

The options a newcomer actually weighs, described by what each one is rather than how it markets itself. The last column is the experience needed to hold the credential, not to sit the exam.

Path What it certifies Who it suits Breadth Experience to be certified
GRC foundation course A taught grounding in how the function works Someone entering GRC from any route Broad — the function end to end (varies by provider) None
ISO 27001 Lead Implementer / Auditor Competence to implement or audit one standard Someone standing up or auditing an ISMS Narrow — a single standard Scheme-dependent: provisional grades none, full lead grades several years
ISACA CISA Information systems audit, governance and control Auditors and audit-adjacent roles Specialised — the audit seat Five years in IS audit, control or security; up to three waivable
ISACA CRISC IT risk identification and control Risk-register and control practitioners Specialised — the risk seat Three years across two or more of four domains; no waivers
ISACA CISM Information security management Practitioners moving into a security-management role Specialised — the management seat Five years in information security, three of them in security management
ISC2 CISSP Broad security across eight domains Security generalists and leads Broad in security, thin on GRC Five years across two or more of the eight domains; one year waivable
SANS / GIAC Hands-on technical skill in a chosen domain Practitioners doing the technical work Deep and domain-specific; some management and audit tracks too GIAC exams: none formal

The credential exams — CISA, CRISC, CISM and CISSP — can each be sat before that experience is complete, but the certification itself waits on it. Read the last column as a destination, not a starting line.

Two patterns. First, every credential in the table is either specialised — the audit seat, the risk seat, the management seat, one standard, one technical domain — or, in CISSP’s case, broad across security engineering rather than across governance, risk and compliance. None of them is a general grounding in the GRC function itself.

Second, all of them assume experience a newcomer does not yet have. They are things you work toward from inside a seat, while the experience accrues, not things you enter the field holding.

What a person entering GRC needs first is the opposite shape: a working map of the whole function — the four artefacts, how a register is scored, what an auditor asks for — that assumes nothing and is tied to no single standard or vendor. With a target seat already in view, the matching credential can come first; without one, the grounding comes first, because a specialist exam taken with no context to attach it to does not stick.

blocks.text: Sequencing, which matters more than choice

blocks.html:
The order tends to beat the pick. If you already know the seat you are heading for, the matching credential is a reasonable first move: CISA for audit, CRISC for an IT-risk role, CISM once you are in a security-management role, an ISO lead course if your first job is standing up an ISMS. If you do not, start with the general grounding and one real artefact you have handled — the walk-through in 6.1 — then choose.

Certifications do most of their work at the screening stage, where a recognised acronym gets a CV read; they do less in the interview, where a specific artefact you can walk through tends to carry more weight than a badge. How that balance falls is employer-dependent, but it is worth knowing which investment does which job.

items.q: What is the best GRC certification?
items.html: There is no single best one, because the certifications answer different questions. CISA is the credential most often asked for in audit-facing roles, CRISC maps to the risk seat, CISM to a security-management role, and CISSP to broad security leadership. For someone entering GRC without a seat in mind, breadth matters more than any one exam: a grounding in the whole function, taken before the specialist badge, is what makes the badge worth having.

items.q: Which GRC certification should I get first?
items.html: If you know the role you are targeting, the credential that matches it. If you do not, usually none first — start with a broad grounding in how the function works and one real artefact you have handled, then choose the certification that fits the seat you are moving toward. A specialist exam taken with no context is hard to retain.

items.q: Is CISA worth it for GRC?
items.html: For audit-adjacent GRC roles it is among the most commonly requested credentials, and it sets no formal education or technical-role prerequisite. Note the experience requirement: five years of IS audit, control or security work, with up to three years of permitted substitutions. You can sit the exam earlier; certification waits on the experience.

items.q: Is CISSP a GRC certification?
items.html: No. CISSP is a broad information-security certification across eight domains. One of them — security and risk management — covers governance, risk and compliance directly, but the certification as a whole is security engineering and leadership rather than GRC operational work, and it does not centre on the artefacts a GRC seat produces.

items.q: Do I need a certification to get into GRC?
items.html: No. A certification helps pass the CV screen; it does not close an interview. A candidate who can walk through one risk they assessed — how it was scored, who owned it, what evidence closed it — tends to outperform one with certificates and nothing to describe. Build the artefact either way.

entries.title: How a GRC career progresses
entries.description: Analyst to manager to head is a change in what you own, not a bigger version of the same job. What earns each move, how long it takes, and where people stall.
keywords: how to get promoted in GRC
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

blocks.html:
Progression in GRC is not doing more of the analyst job faster. Each move up
hands you a different thing to own — first a framework, then a programme, then
the board’s picture of risk — and the people who stall are usually the ones
doing the lower job extremely well.
The ladder has three real rungs, whatever the titles in between suggest. What separates them is not time served but what you can be handed without supervision.

Analyst to manager. The analyst runs the register, chases evidence and completes questionnaires — work measured on whether the artefacts are current and legible. The manager owns a framework end to end and the audit relationship that comes with it. The step is the first time you carry a right to say no: to a control owner, to a timeline, to a scope. Nobody hands that over because you processed questionnaires quickly; they hand it over once you have shown judgement about which risks matter and which findings are worth the fight.

Manager to head. The manager answers for a framework; the head answers for the programme and the narrative the board hears. The work shifts from controls to resourcing, from the audit to the story of the function’s risk position. This is the move where technical fluency stops being the constraint and political literacy starts — the head who cannot get a budget conversation to land is limited regardless of how well they understand the controls.

The sideways move. More common than either, and not a demotion. Risk to privacy, compliance to internal audit, GRC to security architecture or into product. Each rebuilds depth in a new domain on top of the general grounding, and a person with two domains behind them is worth more than one with a single deep specialisation, particularly on the route into consulting.

Not certifications, and not tenure. The signal is the same at every rung: an artefact you owned and a decision you made that turned out to be right.

The analyst earns the manager seat by showing judgement — pushing back on a finding, spotting a risk before it was raised, running a piece of the framework without being told the next step. The manager earns the head seat by owning an outcome the board saw: an audit that produced no surprises, a risk position that matched reality when it was tested. Each move is granted on evidence of the next job, done early, not on mastery of the current one.

The permanent analyst is the common one: someone excellent at the mechanics who never develops the judgement calls that the next seat is made of. The mechanics are visible and rewarded, so it is comfortable to stay, and the register keeps running. The way out is to start making the calls before you are asked to — form a view on which risks matter, argue a finding, own a decision — because the seat is granted to people already doing its work, not promised to people who have earned a turn.

The second plateau is the specialist who went deep too early, built a career on one framework, and finds the head-of-function role wants breadth they traded away. Depth is valuable and it is also a ceiling if it is the only thing you have.

items.q: How long does it take to go from analyst to manager?
items.html: There is no fixed number, because the move is granted on demonstrated judgement rather than years served. Some make it inside two years by owning real decisions early; others run the register competently for longer without ever showing the judgement the next seat requires. Time is a weak predictor; what you have owned is a strong one.

items.q: Do I need a certification to get promoted in GRC?
items.html: Rarely for the move itself. Certifications help you get hired and pass CV screens; promotion turns on whether you have shown you can do the next job. A certification that matches your target seat — CISM heading into management, CRISC into a risk role — can support the case, but it does not make it. See 6.3.

items.q: Is GRC manager a technical role?
items.html: Usually it shifts away from hands-on work rather than toward it: the job is owning a framework, the audit relationship and a set of decisions, and the constraint is judgement more than technical depth. How much fluency it needs still varies by organisation and domain — a manager over cloud or product controls reads more architecture than one over policy and third-party risk. You need enough to challenge an engineer’s answer either way.

entries.title: A day in the life of a GRC analyst
entries.description: What a GRC analyst does all week — questionnaires, evidence chasing, register updates and one hard conversation. How technical it is depends on the seat.
keywords: day in the life GRC analyst
what does a GRC analyst do
sources: ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

blocks.html:
Most of a GRC analyst’s week is turning other people’s work into a record
somebody can act on months later, when the person who did the work is not in the
room. It is writing-heavy, meeting-heavy and deadline-driven, and for a typical
compliance-facing seat far less of it is hands-on technical than people expect.

The rhythm is a steady cadence of recurring work with periodic spikes around audits and questionnaires, not a queue of tickets. Knowing which kind of work is in front of you is most of managing the week.
Some things come round on a cycle whether or not anything has happened.

items.html: Keeping risk entries current — chasing owners for updates, moving review dates, flagging anything that has drifted past its date. The register is only as trustworthy as its most stale row.

Collecting the artefacts that show a control operated — an access review, a change record, a backup test — and filing them so they are legible to someone who was not there. The habit, not the collection, is the skill.
Nudging policies through their review dates, tracking exceptions and waivers, keeping the set consistent when one document changes.
The routine control checks that recur monthly or quarterly, where the work is noticing the exception in a list that is mostly fine.

blocks.html:
Then there is the work that arrives, usually with a date attached.

A security questionnaire from a prospect’s procurement team, which has to be answered accurately and fast because a deal is waiting on it. An audit window, where weeks of collected evidence get assembled, gaps get closed under time pressure, and the analyst is the person who knows where everything is. A new obligation — a contract clause, a regulation, a customer requirement — that has to be mapped to a control before anyone can say whether it is met.

The triggered work is where the recurring work pays off: an analyst who kept the evidence current all quarter has a calm audit week, and one who did not has a bad one.

Nearly every week contains a version of the same conversation: a control owner who has not produced what you asked for. The skill is not escalation — it is finding out why first (usually the request was ambiguous or the system cannot produce it), making the ask specific and easy, and keeping a record. Most of the job’s friction lives in this exchange, and handling it well is what separates a useful analyst from an irritating one.

Three things, consistently. It is writing-heavy — the output is documents and records, not configurations. For a typical compliance-facing seat it is not hands-on technical; you read systems and challenge answers rather than build them, though analysts embedded with a cloud, identity or data team do need that depth. And it is deadline-driven in bursts rather than uniformly busy, with quiet cadence weeks and intense audit weeks. The tools are a GRC platform, a spreadsheet and a ticketing system — the platform matters less than the discipline behind what goes into it.

items.q: Is GRC work boring?
items.html: It is administrative in stretches and it is not a coding job, so people expecting constant technical problem-solving find the cadence work slow. What keeps it engaging for the people who stay is the judgement — deciding which risks matter, handling the control-owner conversation, seeing the whole organisation’s exposure in a way few other seats do.

items.q: What does a GRC analyst do all day?
items.html: Keeps the register current, collects and files evidence, answers security questionnaires, runs recurring control checks, and chases the people whose work those records depend on. Most of the day is turning other people’s activity into a record that will hold up later.

items.q: How technical is a GRC analyst role?
items.html: It depends on the seat. A typical compliance-facing analyst needs to be literate rather than hands-on: read a system diagram, understand what a control does, and challenge an engineer’s answer without accepting it whole, without configuring the system or writing code. An analyst embedded with a cloud or platform team may need real technical depth — cloud IAM, logging, scripting. See 6.0 for how that changes across the seats.

pages.editorial_policy:
Editorial policy

How entries are written, who reviews them, and what gets corrected.

1WHO WRITES THIS

Entries are written by practitioners who have done the work being described — run the register, sat the audit, written the policy that was later tested. Every entry names its editor and the credential they hold. An entry with no named editor is not published.

2REVIEW CYCLE

Each entry carries a review date and an edition number. Entries are reviewed quarterly, and sooner when a source standard is revised. The review date is the date a human read the entry against its sources, not the date a file changed.

3SOURCES

Claims about a framework cite the framework. Where an entry states a practice rather than a requirement, it says so. We do not cite vendor marketing, and we do not cite ourselves.

4CORRECTIONS

Corrections are published, not quietly patched. A corrected entry increments its edition and records what changed. If you have found an error, the fastest route is the “Suggest an edit” link in the header.
